# Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

The war that COMUSMACV inherits on 1 January 1964 is an advisory war that is being lost. Two months earlier the coup of 1 November 1963 had killed Ngo Dinh Diem and his brother Nhu, and with them went the province chiefs, the Strategic Hamlet Program and most of the administrative continuity the Republic of Vietnam possessed. The Military Assistance Command, Vietnam, under General Paul D. Harkins, is a headquarters of advisers, helicopter companies and support troops; the United States has about 23,300 military personnel in the country by the end of 1964 [H40], none of them formed into combat units, and 147 die by hostile action that year [H40]. The fighting is done by the Army of the Republic of Vietnam, the Regional and Popular Forces, and the Civilian Irregular Defense Group camps of the US Special Forces, against a Viet Cong movement that has rebuilt itself since 1959 on the political infrastructure left from the war against France and on cadres regrouped to the North in 1954 and now returning down the Trail.

Phase I runs from January 1964 to the end of July 1965. Its shape is a double collapse and a double response. In Saigon, the state comes apart: between January 1964 and June 1965 the government changes hands by coup or forced resignation repeatedly, and the generals spend more of their energy on each other than on the countryside. In the field, the Viet Cong move from the guerrilla phase to the mobile-war phase, forming regiments and then a division in the provinces around Saigon, and at Binh Gia, Song Be, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai they destroy ARVN battalions in set-piece battles. In Hanoi, the Politburo decides that the moment for decisive victory has come and commits regular PAVN regiments to the South for the first time. The American response comes in two steps: from the air, beginning with the reprisal strikes of August 1964 and February 1965 and hardening into Rolling Thunder in March 1965; and on the ground, beginning with two Marine battalions sent to guard an airfield in March 1965 and ending with the President's decision of July 1965 to commit US ground forces to the war in strength.

Every one of the political constraints that will shape the war is drawn in this phase: the restricted zones around Hanoi and Haiphong, the bar on ground operations in Laos and Cambodia, the reliance on presidential approval for targets in the North, and the decision to fight without calling up the reserves. So is the enemy's basic answer to American firepower: the decision to close in, choose the time of battle, and keep his base areas beyond the border.

## ◆ EV000-1 · Khanh's coup · 30 Jan 1964 · Saigon · HIST · 000
Before dawn on 30 January 1964 Major General Nguyen Khanh, commanding I Corps, took power from the Military Revolutionary Council of General Duong Van Minh without firing a shot [H8]. He acted with Generals Tran Thien Khiem and Nguyen Van Thieu and Colonels Nguyen Chanh Thi and Do Mau [H8]. Generals Tran Van Don, Le Van Kim, Ton That Dinh and Mai Huu Xuan were put under house arrest on a charge of plotting a French-backed neutralist settlement, and Prime Minister Nguyen Ngoc Tho was detained [H8]. The one death was Major Nguyen Van Nhung, Minh's aide, executed after the takeover [H8]. Khanh kept Minh as a figurehead chief of state [H8]. The generals were tried in closed session on 28–29 May and found guilty only of "lax morality" [H8].

Washington was surprised but quick to back the new man; President Johnson sent Khanh a personal note on 2 February [H8]. The coup mattered less for what Khanh did than for the precedent it set: a second violent change of government within three months, carried out by officers against officers, and accepted by the United States. Province and district chiefs appointed after November 1963 were replaced again, and the pacification apparatus, already broken by the abandonment of the Strategic Hamlet Program, lost what continuity remained. In March, Secretary of Defense McNamara visited and endorsed Khanh, and NSAM 288 of 17 March 1964 committed the United States to the survival of an independent, non-communist South Vietnam [H]. In June 1964 General William C. Westmoreland, Harkins's deputy since January, took command of MACV, and General Maxwell D. Taylor replaced Henry Cabot Lodge as ambassador in July [H].

## ◆ EV000-2 · The battle of Nam Dong · 6 Jul 1964 · Nam Dong CIDG camp, about 50 km west of Da Nang near the Laotian border · HIST · 000
At 02:30 on 6 July 1964 a force that the Americans estimated at about two battalions of Viet Cong and PAVN, some 800–900 men [H4], attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong in the mountains west of Da Nang, near the Laotian border. The camp was held by Special Forces Detachment A-726 under Captain Roger H. C. Donlon, 12 Americans in all, with one Australian warrant officer of the Australian Army Training Team Vietnam, 311 Montagnard strikers, 50 Nung mercenaries and seven Vietnamese Special Forces [H4]. The attack opened with mortar fire on the command post and a sapper assault on the main gate; the outer perimeter was penetrated and many strikers deserted or went over to the attackers [H4].

The inner perimeter, held by the Americans and the Nungs, survived about five hours of close fighting until the attackers withdrew at dawn [H4]. Two Americans and the Australian adviser were killed; 58 strikers and Nungs died and 57 were wounded, and more than 100 strikers defected [H4]. Fifty-five to sixty-two attackers' bodies were counted around the wire [H4], a figure more reliable than most body counts because the dead lay inside a perimeter the defenders held. Donlon, wounded several times, became the first American awarded the Medal of Honor in Vietnam [H4]. Nam Dong is the pattern of the border camp war: an isolated garrison of irregulars whose loyalty is uncertain, a night assault by a force that has chosen its moment, no reinforcement before daylight, and a defence that survives on the quality of a handful of men.

## ◆ EV000-3 · The Gulf of Tonkin incidents and the Southeast Asia Resolution · 2–10 Aug 1964 · Gulf of Tonkin and Washington · HIST · 000
On 30–31 July 1964 South Vietnamese commando boats under the covert OPLAN 34A programme, run by MACV's Studies and Observations Group, raided the North Vietnamese islands of Hon Me and Hon Ngu [H7]. On 2 August the destroyer USS *Maddox*, on a DESOTO signals intelligence patrol under Captain John J. Herrick, was attacked in daylight by three P-4 torpedo boats of the 135th Torpedo Squadron [H7]. The *Maddox* fired, four F-8 Crusaders from USS *Ticonderoga* attacked the retiring boats, and the North Vietnamese lost four killed and six wounded with three boats damaged; the *Maddox* was struck by one machine-gun round and suffered no casualties [H7].

On the night of 4 August the *Maddox* and USS *Turner Joy*, in rough weather, fired for about two hours at radar contacts they took to be a second attack. Herrick cabled that the "entire action leaves many doubts" [H7]. No wreckage or bodies were found, and the National Security Agency's own history, written in 2001 and declassified in 2005, concluded that no attack took place and that signals intelligence had been presented selectively [H7]. Johnson decided on retaliation within thirty minutes [H7]. On 5 August, in Operation Pierce Arrow, 64 sorties from USS *Ticonderoga* and USS *Constellation* struck torpedo-boat bases and the oil storage at Vinh [H]. Two aircraft were lost; Lieutenant (jg) Richard Sather was killed and Lieutenant (jg) Everett Alvarez became the first American naval aviator taken prisoner by North Vietnam [H].

On 7 August Congress passed the Southeast Asia Resolution, 416–0 in the House and 88–2 in the Senate, authorizing the President to take "all necessary steps, including the use of armed force" [H7] [H]. Johnson signed it on 10 August [H]. It was the only legislative authority for the war that followed. B-57B bombers were moved to Bien Hoa in the aftermath [H3], within mortar range of the countryside around it.

## ◆ EV000-4 · The Vung Tau Charter crisis and the September coup attempt · 16 Aug – 14 Sep 1964 · Saigon, Hue and Da Nang · HIST · 000
Khanh tried to use the Tonkin crisis to make himself president under a new constitution, the Vung Tau Charter of 16 August 1964 [H] [H10]. Students and the Buddhist movement led by Thich Tri Quang answered with demonstrations and riots in Saigon, Hue and Da Nang, and Khanh conceded the repeal of the charter [H10]. At a Military Revolutionary Council meeting on 26–27 August he promised to resign, but the generals could agree on no successor, and a triumvirate of Khanh, Minh and Khiem was formed to rule for two months; Khanh dominated it [H10]. Khiem was sent abroad as ambassador to Washington and Minh on a "goodwill tour" [H10].

Before dawn on 13 September Generals Lam Van Phat and Duong Van Duc, with about ten battalions recruited among them and four moving up from the Mekong Delta, seized key points in Saigon and announced a new government on the radio while Khanh took refuge in Da Lat [H10]. The coup collapsed within a day. US officials publicly backed Khanh; Air Commodore Nguyen Cao Ky, commanding the Vietnamese Air Force, flew jets low over the city and brought loyal marines and paratroopers into Tan Son Nhut, and General Nguyen Chanh Thi supported him; Phat and Duc backed down on the morning of 14 September [H10]. No one was killed [H10]. The lasting result was a new power centre: the younger officers, the "Young Turks" around Ky and Thi, who had saved Khanh and now knew they could unmake him [H10]. The war in the countryside was left to commanders whose first concern was the next coup.

## ◆ EV000-5 · The Hop Tac programme · Sep 1964 – mid-1965 · Saigon and the surrounding provinces · HIST · 000
In September 1964, at the urging of the US Mission and Westmoreland, the government launched Hop Tac ("cooperation"), a plan to pacify a ring of territory around Saigon outward in phases, the "oil spot" concept applied to the capital region [H] [H25]. The priority was explicit: concentrate resources on the Saigon area and accept little progress elsewhere for the time being [H25]. By then the trend elsewhere was plain. Ambassador Taylor's mission reported on 6 October that the provinces rated unsatisfactory for pacification had risen from 7 in July to 14 in August, and named the diversion of resources to Hop Tac as one possible cause [H25]. The mission nonetheless recommended unanimously that Hop Tac be given full support [H25].

The programme never reached its schedule. Its ARVN units were repeatedly pulled away by coups and coup alerts, its Vietnamese chain of command changed with each government, and the Viet Cong infrastructure in Gia Dinh, Long An and the provinces north of the capital was left largely intact [H]. By mid-1965 Hop Tac was effectively moribund [H]. Its failure foreshadowed the problem of the whole war: pacification required a stable government and a security force that would stay in the hamlets at night, and in 1964 the Republic of Vietnam had neither.

## ◆ EV000-6 · Hanoi commits the regulars; the Trail and the first air war in Laos · Sep 1964 – Apr 1965 · North Vietnam, the Laotian panhandle and the Central Highlands · HIST · 000
The Ninth Plenum of the Lao Dong Party Central Committee, in December 1963, had resolved to seek a decisive military victory in the South before the United States could intervene in strength [H]. Through 1964 the Politburo under Le Duan acted on it. Infiltration down the Trail, managed since 1959 by the PAVN's Group 559, shifted from regrouped southerners to northern-born conscripts, and in the autumn of 1964 the first complete PAVN regular regiments were ordered south [H]. The 95th Regiment of the 325th Division arrived in Kontum Province in December 1964; the 101st Regiment followed in February 1965 with the division commander, Colonel Nguyen Huu An; the 18th Regiment came a few months later [H22]. The division was then broken up among the B3 (Central Highlands) Front and Military Region 5 [H22]. These were the first regular North Vietnamese formations committed to the war, and by the US estimate of 1965 about 4,500 PAVN troops and 300 tons of materiel moved through Laos each month [H24]. Both figures are intelligence estimates of their time; the movement was disciplined, at night, under canopy and through a country that US ground forces could not enter.

The American answer in Laos began on 14 December 1964 with Operation Barrel Roll, a small programme of armed reconnaissance by US aircraft over northern and eastern Laos [H24]. On 3 April 1965 the 2nd Air Division opened Operation Steel Tiger against the Trail in the southeastern panhandle [H24]. Both were bound by the fiction of Laotian neutrality under the Geneva Accords of 1962, by the ambassador in Vientiane's control of targets, and by the bar on ground operations across the border. The Trail at this stage was still largely foot and bicycle traffic with truck routes being built; its capacity was growing faster than anything flying over it could reduce.

## ◆ EV000-7 · The attack on Bien Hoa air base · 1 Nov 1964 · Bien Hoa air base, Bien Hoa Province · HIST · 000
On the night of 31 October–1 November 1964, two days before the American presidential election, a Viet Cong mortar team fired on Bien Hoa air base, about 30 km northeast of Saigon, for about thirty minutes [H2]. The B-57B Canberras moved there after the Tonkin crisis were parked wingtip to wingtip on the ramp. Five B-57Bs were destroyed and 13 damaged; with helicopters and other aircraft, as many as 30 aircraft were destroyed or damaged [H2] [H3]. Four Americans were killed and 72 people wounded [H2]. The attackers escaped.

It was the first of at least 475 attacks on the primary air bases in South Vietnam during the war [H2]. Ambassador Taylor and the Joint Chiefs pressed for reprisal bombing of the North; Johnson, on the eve of the election, declined [H]. The attack exposed what American airpower in South Vietnam would cost: every base needed a ground perimeter that the ARVN could not or would not hold, and the question of who would guard the bases was the question that would bring the first US combat troops ashore four months later.

## ◆ EV000-8 · The Brink Hotel bombing and the purge of the High National Council · 19–24 Dec 1964 · Saigon · HIST · 000
In the week before Christmas the Young Turks, with Khanh's acquiescence, dissolved the High National Council, the civilian body set up to give the government a constitutional face, and arrested several of its members [H10]. Ambassador Taylor summoned the officers and dressed them down; Khanh answered by attacking Taylor publicly, and relations between the US Mission and the junta reached their low point [H10]. The civilian prime minister, Tran Van Huong, who had held office since early November, was left without authority [H].

At 17:45 on 24 December a charge of about 90 kg of explosive in a car parked beneath the Brink Bachelor Officers' Quarters in central Saigon exploded during the evening gathering in the officers' bar [H20]. Two Americans were killed, Lieutenant Colonel James R. Hagen and a Navy Department civilian, David M. Agnew; the wounded are given variously as 38 American officers and 25 Vietnamese civilians, 58 people, or 98, and are best stated as about 60–100 [H20]. Two Viet Cong operatives, disguised as a driver and an ARVN major, placed the car and escaped [H20]. Taylor and Westmoreland urged reprisal strikes; Johnson again refused, doubting that the public would accept Viet Cong responsibility and saying that he had "never felt that this war will be won from the air" [H20]. Within six weeks he had changed his mind.

## ◆ EV000-9 · The battle of Binh Gia · 28 Dec 1964 – 1 Jan 1965 · Binh Gia, Phuoc Tuy Province · HIST · 000
Binh Gia, a Catholic village of northern refugees in Phuoc Tuy Province east of Saigon, was the site of the Viet Cong's first large set-piece battle [H1]. The attackers were the 271st and 272nd Regiments (then called the 1st and 2nd), the nucleus of the forming 9th Division, with the 80th Artillery Detachment and local battalions of the B-2 Front, an estimated 1,800 men [H1]. They took the village on 28 December and then waited for the relief. The ARVN committed the 30th, 33rd, 35th and 38th Ranger Battalions and the 4th Marine Battalion of the general reserve, with two artillery platoons and a section of M24 tanks, about 4,300 men [H1], lifted and supported by the US 118th Aviation Company and the gunships of the 68th Assault Helicopter Company [H1].

The relieving battalions were fed in piecemeal, the artillery badly positioned and air support thin [H1]. On 30 December a 68th Company gunship was shot down near Quang Giao and its four crewmen killed [H1]; on 31 December the 4th Marine Battalion, going to recover the bodies, was ambushed in a rubber plantation and destroyed, losing 122 killed including its commander, Major Nguyen Van Nho, and 71 wounded [H1]. MACV counted allied losses from 28 December to 6 January at 201 killed, 192 wounded and 68 missing, including five Americans dead and three missing or captured, among them Captain Donald Cook, the Marine adviser, who died in captivity [H1]. MACV reported four helicopters shot down [H1]. The VC claimed 1,783 killed and captured and 35 helicopters destroyed, which is not credible; their own losses are given only as at least 32 confirmed dead, which is a floor and not an estimate [H1].

The significance was not the arithmetic but the form. A Viet Cong formation had held ground for four days against armour, artillery and helicopters, defeated the general reserve, and withdrawn intact [H1]. The 271st took the honorific "Binh Gia Regiment" [H1]. US observers concluded that the ARVN could not defeat main-force units of this kind without American firepower and, increasingly, without American troops.

## ◆ EV000-10 · The fall of Khanh · 27 Jan – 25 Feb 1965 · Saigon · HIST · 000
On 27 January 1965 Khanh and the Armed Forces Council removed Prime Minister Huong after another wave of Buddhist protest [H]. On 16 February, to stop Khanh installing a prime minister of his own choosing, the council appointed Dr Phan Huy Quat, a civilian physician and former foreign minister [H23]. On 19–20 February Colonel Pham Ngoc Thao and General Lam Van Phat attempted another coup; it failed, but in its confusion the Armed Forces Council, with American encouragement, voted Khanh out [H23] [H10]. He left the country on 25 February with the title of roving ambassador [H]. Thao, who went into hiding, was a communist agent, as later became clear [H].

Quat's civilian cabinet governed under the oversight of a military council in which Ky and Thieu were now the strongest figures [H23]. The government that would receive the American ground commitment was a caretaker administration whose authority depended on generals who had just shown that they would remove anyone, and whose own legitimacy with the population of the countryside was close to nil.

## ◆ EV000-11 · Pleiku, Qui Nhon and Flaming Dart · 7–11 Feb 1965 · Camp Holloway and Pleiku, Pleiku Province; Qui Nhon, Binh Dinh Province; southern North Vietnam · HIST · 000
At 01:50 on 7 February 1965, while the President's national security adviser McGeorge Bundy was in Saigon and Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin was in Hanoi [H], about 300 men of the 30th Company of the VC 409th Sapper Battalion, reinforced by local engineers and a local force company and issued four 81mm mortars, attacked the US Army helicopter base at Camp Holloway and the advisers' compound at Pleiku [H5]. Seven Americans were killed and 104 wounded; 10 aircraft were destroyed and 15 damaged [H5]. Bundy recommended reprisal from Saigon, and about twelve hours after the attack 49 aircraft from USS *Coral Sea* and USS *Hancock* struck the barracks at Dong Hoi just north of the 17th parallel, the first strike of Operation Flaming Dart [H5].

On 10 February the VC blew up the enlisted men's billet at Qui Nhon, killing 23 Americans [H5]. On 11 February about 160 US and Vietnamese aircraft struck the barracks at Chanh Hoa and Chap Le in the southern North [H5]. Flaming Dart was still framed as reprisal for specific attacks, but Bundy's report of 7 February argued for "sustained reprisal" against the North as the best available way to affect the war, and the administration accepted it [H]. Pleiku is the hinge of the phase: within four weeks the reprisal policy had become a continuing bombing campaign.

## ◆ EV000-12 · Rolling Thunder begins · 2 Mar 1965 · North Vietnam, south of the 20th parallel · HIST · 000
On 2 March 1965 Operation Rolling Thunder opened with a strike by 104 USAF aircraft, F-105s, F-100s and B-57s, on the ammunition storage area near Xom Bang, while 19 RVNAF A-1 Skyraiders struck the naval base at Quang Khe [H9]. It was conceived as a graduated campaign: a slowly rising pressure on the North, moving northward a step at a time, meant to signal resolve, raise the cost of supporting the insurgency and bring Hanoi to negotiate, while avoiding Chinese or Soviet intervention [H].

The constraints were part of the design. Targets were chosen in Washington, approved individually by the President and the Secretary of Defense at the weekly meetings of the "Tuesday" group, which also fixed timing, numbers of aircraft and ordnance [H9]. Strikes were barred within 30 nautical miles of Hanoi and 10 of Haiphong and in a 30-mile buffer along the Chinese frontier [H9]. The North was divided into route packages assigned to the Air Force and the Navy [H9]. North Vietnam began the campaign with about 1,500 anti-aircraft guns and a few dozen MiG-17s; the United States estimated more than 5,000 guns within a year [H9]. Through 24 December 1965 the USAF flew 25,971 sorties and dropped 32,063 tons and the Navy flew 28,168 sorties and dropped 11,144 tons, at a cost of 180 US aircraft [H9]. The campaign that began on 2 March would last, with pauses, until November 1968.

## ◆ EV000-13 · The Marines land at Da Nang · 8 Mar – 6 May 1965 · Da Nang, Quang Nam Province · HIST · 000
On 8 March 1965 Battalion Landing Team 3/9 under Lieutenant Colonel Charles E. McPartlin came ashore over Red Beach 2 northwest of Da Nang, an hour late because of surf, and the first C-130s carrying BLT 1/3 under Lieutenant Colonel Herbert J. Bain landed from Okinawa at about 13:00; the airlift halted and resumed, and 1/3 was complete by 12 March [H15]. The 9th Marine Expeditionary Brigade under Brigadier General Frederick J. Karch numbered nearly 5,000 [H15]. Its mission was the security of Da Nang air base, which Rolling Thunder now needed and the Bien Hoa attack had shown to be vulnerable [H14]. The Joint Chiefs' orders were that the Marines "will not, repeat will not, engage in day-to-day actions against the Viet Cong" [H15].

The restriction lasted three weeks. At a National Security Council meeting on 1 April the President approved the use of Marines "in active combat under conditions to be established and approved by the Secretary of Defense" and an increase of 18,000–20,000 in US support forces [H15]. In April further battalion landing teams arrived [H15]; on 6 May the brigade became the III Marine Amphibious Force [H14]. The enclave concept, US forces holding coastal bases and patrolling outward, was the first form of American ground strategy and lasted only until the summer. By the end of 1965 III MAF would number more than 38,000 [H15].

## ◆ EV000-14 · The bombing of the US embassy · 30 Mar 1965 · Saigon · HIST · 000
On 30 March 1965 a car packed with about 300 pounds of plastic explosive was parked outside the US embassy; a Vietnamese policeman who argued with the driver was shot by a second VC who drove up alongside, before the charge exploded [H12]. Twenty-two people were killed, two Americans, among them Barbara Robbins of the CIA, 19 Vietnamese and a Filipino serving in the US Navy, and 183 were wounded [H12]. Johnson rejected calls for a specific reprisal; Rolling Thunder was already running [H12]. Congress voted one million dollars for a new, fortified embassy, which opened on 29 September 1967 [H12]. The bombing confirmed that the VC could strike anywhere in Saigon and that its urban networks were intact after a decade of police effort.

## ◆ EV000-15 · The Thanh Hoa Bridge and the northern air defences · 3 Apr – 24 Jul 1965 · Thanh Hoa (Ham Rong), Thanh Hoa Province, and the Hanoi region · HIST · 000
On 3 April 1965 a 79-aircraft package led by Lieutenant Colonel Robinson Risner, 46 F-105s with F-100 escorts, RF-101Cs and KC-135 tankers, attacked the Ham Rong bridge over the Song Ma at Thanh Hoa; 16 F-105s carried AGM-12 Bullpup missiles and the rest 750 lb bombs [H16]. The bridge was hit repeatedly and stood; traffic stopped for a few hours; an F-100 and an RF-101 were lost [H16]. On 4 April 48 F-105s returned with 750 lb bombs. Eight MiG-17s of the VPAF 921st Fighter Regiment, half acting as decoys, attacked the F-105s and shot down two, killing Major Frank Bennett and Captain J. A. Magnusson; a third F-105, Captain Carlyle Harris's, was lost and its pilot captured [H16]. The VPAF lost three MiG-17 pilots that day; how each was lost is disputed [H16]. The bridge, struck by more than 300 bombs, still stood; it would stand until laser-guided bombs dropped its span in 1972 [H16].

On 24 July an SA-2 Guideline missile shot down an F-4C near the munitions depot at Dien Bien Phu, the first US aircraft lost to a surface-to-air missile [H9]. Within five months the North's air defence had become an integrated system of guns, MiGs, radar and missiles, and the restricted zone around Hanoi had become its sanctuary.

## ◆ EV000-16 · The battle of Song Be · 10–12 May 1965 · Song Be (Phuoc Long province capital) and Phuoc Binh, Phuoc Long Province · HIST · 000
The 173rd Airborne Brigade, the first US Army combat formation in the country, began arriving at Bien Hoa and Vung Tau on 5 May 1965 to guard the air bases [H]. Five days later the VC opened their summer offensive. In the early hours of 11 May B-2 Front forces, identified variously as the 763rd Regiment with the 840th Battalion or as elements of the 271st–273rd Regiments, with two sapper platoons and artillery, attacked Song Be, capital of Phuoc Long Province, 119 km northeast of Saigon, and the district town of Phuoc Binh [H13]. The defence rested on the 36th Ranger Battalion, about 250 men, about 150 territorials, and about three dozen American advisers, mostly of Special Forces Detachment B-34 under Lieutenant Colonel Alton E. Park, who was badly wounded; Major Mitchell A. Sakely took over [H13]. Gunships of the US 197th Aviation Company supported them, and a relieving Ranger battalion reached the town by midday on 11 May [H13].

The town was held. The ARVN lost 58 killed, 96 wounded and 83 missing; five Americans were killed and 13 wounded; a B-57 was shot down; civilian dead are given as 12–80 [H13]. The advisers counted 297 VC dead, and MACV estimated up to 1,000 VC killed and wounded, which is an estimate of the kind A13 warns against [H13]. The communist history claims 1,389 allied killed, including 30 Americans, which is fiction [H13]. Song Be was a battle the government won, narrowly and with American firepower; the next two were not.

## ◆ EV000-17 · The battle of Ba Gia · 28–31 May 1965 · Ba Gia, Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province · HIST · 000
On 29 May 1965 the VC 1st Regiment of the forming 2nd Division (40th, 60th and 90th Battalions, with the 45th Independent Battalion and local force battalions), directed by PAVN Major General Chu Huy Man, overran the outpost at Loc Tho near Ba Gia, about 10 km from Quang Ngai, and ambushed and destroyed the ARVN 1st Battalion, 51st Infantry Regiment as it came to help [H11]. Major General Nguyen Chanh Thi, commanding I Corps, sent a task force under the 51st Regiment: its 2nd Battalion, the 3rd Marine Battalion, the 37th and 39th Ranger Battalions, two 105mm artillery battalions and an M113 squadron [H11]. On 30 May the 39th Rangers fought the VC 45th Battalion on Mount Chop Non, and the 2nd Battalion, 51st and the Marines were hit near Phuoc Loc; US fighter-bombers and UH-1 gunships, delayed because forward air controllers could not find the fight, prevented a rout [H11]. On the night of 30–31 May the 3rd Marines held a moat line through repeated assaults; the 39th Rangers were reduced to a single company [H11]. The VC withdrew at dawn on 31 May.

The US Army's history gives ARVN losses of 107 killed, 123 wounded and 367 captured or missing, with 384 individual and 10 crew-served weapons lost; 84 VC bodies were found and MACV estimated up to 826 VC casualties [H11]. The Vietnamese official account claims 915 ARVN killed or wounded and 270 captured [H11]. Ba Gia was the first time the VC destroyed an ARVN regimental task force, and by 3 June they controlled much of northern Quang Ngai [H11]. On 5 July they overran Ba Gia again, and the ARVN abandoned the post [H11]. In Washington it was read as proof that the ARVN could no longer cope alone.

## ◆ EV000-18 · The battle of Dong Xoai · 9–13 Jun 1965 · Dong Xoai district town and CIDG camp, Phuoc Long Province · HIST · 000
Late on 9 June 1965 the VC 272nd Regiment, with a battalion of the 273rd, a 75mm recoilless rifle company, an 82mm mortar company, a flamethrower company and anti-aircraft machine guns, attacked the district headquarters and CIDG camp at Dong Xoai; the 271st Regiment lay in reserve in the Thuan Loi rubber plantation [H6]. The camp was held by Special Forces Detachment A-342, nine men of Navy Seabee Team 1104, three CIDG companies, the 111th Regional Force Company and militia, with six armoured cars and two 105mm howitzers [H6]. The camp was largely overrun during the night, and the survivors held out in the district headquarters until helicopters of the 118th Aviation Company lifted them out [H6]. On 10 June the 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment (ARVN 5th Division), was landed at Thuan Loi and overwhelmed; the 52nd Ranger Battalion retook the town; on 11 June the 7th Airborne Battalion arrived with about 470 men, and on 12 June the 271st ambushed it and only about 150 came back [H6]. The 145th Aviation Battalion committed every aircraft it had [H6].

The allied figures are 416 South Vietnamese killed, 174 wounded and 233 missing; 18 Americans killed; about 300 civilians killed and 2,500 made refugees [H6]. More than 300 VC bodies and 104 weapons were found and the allies estimated 625 more VC dead; the Vietnamese official account gives 134 killed and 290 wounded [H6]. Second Lieutenant Charles Q. Williams and Construction Mechanic Third Class Marvin G. Shields received the Medal of Honor, Shields posthumously, the only Seabee so honoured [H6]. On 13 June Westmoreland committed the 1st Battalion, 503rd Infantry of the 173rd Airborne Brigade to Phuoc Vinh, the first commitment of US ground troops to a major battle; the VC had already gone, and the battalion returned on 18 June without contact [H6]. After Dong Xoai the ARVN in III Corps had one reserve battalion left [H6].

## ◆ EV000-19 · Quat resigns; the Thieu–Ky government · 12–19 Jun 1965 · Saigon · HIST · 000
On 12 June 1965 Prime Minister Quat, deadlocked with the chief of state Phan Khac Suu over a cabinet reshuffle, handed power back to the military [H23]. On 14 June the generals formed a National Leadership Committee with Major General Nguyen Van Thieu as its chairman and chief of state, and on 19 June Air Vice Marshal Nguyen Cao Ky became prime minister as chairman of the Central Executive Committee [H] [H23]. American officials expected it to last no longer than its predecessors. It lasted the war, in the sense that Thieu would govern until April 1975; but it began as a junta of officers in their thirties and forties with no political base outside the armed forces [H].

## ◆ EV000-20 · The first Arc Light strike · 18 Jun 1965 · Near Ben Cat, Binh Duong Province · HIST · 000
On 18 June 1965 Strategic Air Command flew its first B-52 mission of the war. Thirty B-52s of the 7th and 320th Bombardment Wings were launched from Andersen Air Force Base, Guam [H18] [H19]. Over the sea, while circling to meet their KC-135 tankers, two B-52Fs collided and fell into the sea, killing eight crewmen [H18]. Twenty-seven aircraft struck a suspected Viet Cong base area near Ben Cat, about 40 miles north of Saigon, with 750 lb and 1,000 lb bombs [H18] [H19]. Ground follow-up found little: the enemy had left, or had not been there in strength [H]. The mission was widely ridiculed as a sledgehammer swung at flies [H]. Within five months B-52s would be striking within a few kilometres of US troops in the Ia Drang; Arc Light would continue until August 1973 and fly about 126,615 sorties [H17]. What its first strike showed is the find-and-fix problem in its purest form: unlimited striking power, aimed at a target located by intelligence that was hours or days old.

## ◆ EV000-21 · The July decision · 28 Jul 1965 · Washington · HIST · 000
On 7 June 1965 Westmoreland asked for a major reinforcement to stop what he judged a coming collapse; by 22 July the President had authorized US combat strength of 44 battalions [H11]. On 28 July, at a midday press conference rather than in an address to Congress, Johnson announced that US forces in Vietnam would rise immediately from 75,000 to 125,000, with more to follow as requested, that monthly draft calls would rise over time from 17,000 to 35,000, and that the Airmobile Division would deploy [H21]. The reserves were not called up and no new taxes were sought [H]. The decision was presented as a continuation of policy and made, in effect, without a public debate. Its strategy, Westmoreland's three-phase concept of halting the losing trend in 1965, taking the offensive in high-priority areas in 1966 and destroying the enemy's main forces and base areas thereafter, committed the United States to a war of attrition against an enemy who controlled his own losses by deciding when to fight.

## How the phase ends
By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has destroyed ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security forces it needs.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

---

# Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

Phase II is the American war at full stride. US military strength in Vietnam rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 385,000 at the end of 1966 and 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967 [H40]. The strategy is Westmoreland's: US divisions and brigades, with airmobility and almost unlimited firepower, seek out and destroy the enemy's main-force regiments and base areas, while the ARVN is turned increasingly to territorial security and pacification. The measure of success becomes attrition, the "crossover point" at which the enemy loses men faster than he can replace them through recruitment in the South and infiltration from the North. The instrument of measurement becomes the body count, which inflates at every level of reporting and never once establishes that the crossover has been reached.

The shape of the phase is a series of large operations that win their battles and do not change the war. At the Ia Drang in November 1965 the 1st Cavalry Division meets PAVN regulars in the Central Highlands and both sides draw the lessons they want. In 1966 the operations grow (Masher/White Wing on the Bong Son plain, Hastings below the DMZ, Attleboro in War Zone C) and in 1967 they culminate in the corps-sized sweeps of Cedar Falls and Junction City. Each kills enemy soldiers in numbers the reports exaggerate, captures rice and documents, empties villages, and is followed by the enemy's return when the Americans leave. The enemy decides when to fight; most of the large engagements begin with his attack or his ambush, and he withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. Along the DMZ the war becomes positional: the Marines are drawn from pacification in the coastal hamlets to strongpoints at Con Thien, Gio Linh and Khe Sanh under PAVN artillery fired from the North.

Behind the main-force war, three other wars run. Rolling Thunder grows into the largest bombing campaign since 1945 against a North whose air defences grow with it, and does not stop the flow south. In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta survives the Buddhist uprising of 1966, writes a constitution and wins an election in 1967 with a third of the vote. And the pacification effort, neglected while the divisions fight, is reorganized under a single American manager, CORDS, in May 1967. In Hanoi, meanwhile, the militants around Le Duan conclude that the war of attrition is not being won either, and in the second half of 1967 they plan a general offensive to break it.

## ◆ EV000-22 · Operation Starlite · 18–24 Aug 1965 · Van Tuong peninsula, south of Chu Lai, Quang Ngai Province · HIST · 000
On 15 August 1965 a deserter from the VC 1st Regiment surrendered to the ARVN and, under interrogation at General Thi's I Corps headquarters, gave away the regiment's base on the Van Tuong peninsula, about 12 miles south of the new Marine airfield at Chu Lai, and its plan to attack the field [H26]. III MAF had corroboration from another source [H26]. On 18 August the Marines attacked by land, sea and air: the 3rd Battalion, 3rd Marines came across the beach from the amphibious ships USS *Bayfield*, *Cabildo* and *Vernon County*; the 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines came in by UH-34 helicopters of HMM-261 and HMM-361 to block inland; the 1st and 3rd Battalions, 7th Marines were committed in support and reserve, all under Colonel Oscar F. Peatross of the 7th Marines [H26]. The cruiser USS *Galveston* and destroyers *Orleck* and *Prichett*, A-4s and F-4s of Marine Aircraft Groups 11 and 12 and the 3rd Battalion, 12th Marines supported them [H26]. The VC 1st Regiment, with its 60th and 80th Battalions, a company of the 45th Weapons Battalion and the 52nd Company, under Le Huu Tru, fought from prepared hamlets and ambushed a supply column [H26].

The Marines lost 45 killed and 203 wounded [H26]. They reported 614 VC killed, 9 prisoners, 42 suspects and 109 weapons [H26]; the gap between bodies counted and weapons taken is the first clear instance in this war of a count inflated by its counters. VC accounts admit about 50 killed and some 200 killed, wounded or captured, which is too low [H26]. Corporal Robert E. O'Malley and Lance Corporal Joe C. Paul received the Medal of Honor [H26]. Starlite was the first regimental-sized US battle of the war and a clean tactical victory, won on a piece of human intelligence the war would rarely provide again so cleanly. The 1st Regiment was rebuilt and back in the field within months.

## ◆ EV000-23 · Plei Me and the Ia Drang · 19 Oct – 18 Nov 1965 · Plei Me CIDG camp and the Ia Drang valley below the Chu Pong massif, Pleiku Province · HIST · 000
On 19 October 1965 the PAVN B3 Front under Major General Chu Huy Man attacked the Special Forces camp at Plei Me, south of Pleiku, and the next day ambushed the ARVN relief column; the relief reached the camp at dusk on 25 October and the PAVN withdrew west towards the Chu Pong massif on the Cambodian border [H27]. The 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), newly arrived, was turned loose in pursuit. On 14 November the 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Harold G. Moore air-assaulted into Landing Zone X-Ray at the foot of the Chu Pong, into the assembly area of the 66th Regiment [H27]. For three days the 7th and 9th Battalions of the 66th, with elements of the 33rd, assaulted a perimeter held with the help of the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert Tully, massed tube artillery, tactical air and, from 15 November, B-52s striking about 7 km to the west, the first tactical use of the bombers, in five missions and 96 sorties over the campaign [H27]. American losses at X-Ray were 79 killed and 121 wounded; Moore's count of PAVN dead, reduced by him from 834 to 634, and an estimate of 1,215, are the figures of record [H27].

On 17 November the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert McDade, marching overland to Landing Zone Albany, was ambushed in column in tall grass by the 8th Battalion, 66th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 33rd Regiment [H27]. The PAVN, following Colonel Nguyen Huu An's order to "grab them by the belt", fought inside the column where American artillery and air could not reach them, for about sixteen hours [H27]. The battalion lost 155 killed, 124 wounded and 4 missing, the worst American loss of a single day so far [H27]. Over the campaign the United States counted 237 dead and claimed a kill ratio of nearly ten to one; a PAVN report of 1966 gives 559 killed and 669 wounded [H27]. Both sides inflated the other's losses [H27].

Both commands judged the Ia Drang a success, and each drew the lesson that confirmed its strategy: Westmoreland that airmobile forces with heavy fire support could destroy PAVN regulars at a favourable rate; the PAVN that by closing to close quarters and choosing when to fight they could neutralize American firepower and withdraw across the Cambodian border to rebuild [H27]. McNamara, visiting after the battle, advised the President at the end of November that even a doubling of US forces in 1966 might produce only a military stalemate at a higher level [H].

## ◆ EV000-24 · Operation Masher/White Wing · 24 Jan – 6 Mar 1966 · Bong Son plain and the Kim Son and An Lao valleys, Binh Dinh Province · HIST · 000
In the first large-unit operation of 1966 the 1st Cavalry Division, with the ARVN 22nd Division, an ARVN airborne brigade blocking along Highway 1 and the ROK Capital Division, swept the Bong Son plain and the valleys behind it in northern Binh Dinh, the heartland of the PAVN 3rd (Sao Vang) Division: the 22nd and 12th Regiments and the VC 2nd Regiment, about 6,000 men [H28]. The Marines ran Operation Double Eagle in Quang Ngai to the north, and the Koreans Operation Flying Tiger to the south [H28]. President Johnson had the name changed from Masher to White Wing because the original sounded too brutal [H28].

The division lost 228 killed and 834 wounded, and 46 more men died in a separate aircraft crash; Double Eagle cost the Marines 24 killed and 156 wounded [H28]. The United States claimed 1,342 PAVN and VC killed and the ARVN and Koreans another 808; 254 weapons were recovered [H28]. The disproportion between the two figures drew criticism at the time [H28]. US figures counted more than 27,000 civilians displaced, and of about 8,000 people in the An Lao valley, 4,500 left; a mid-1966 Army study found US and South Vietnamese bombing and artillery to be the main cause of refugee movement in the province [H28]. Civilian deaths are largely unknown; Korean troops of the Capital Division are reported to have killed more than 1,000 civilians at Binh An/Tay Vinh, a figure from Vietnamese sources that has never been tested in any proceeding [H28].

The 3rd Division slipped away, much of it before the operation reached it, and intelligence reported its return to the area about a week after the cavalry withdrew [H28]. The 1st Cavalry came back in Operation Crazy Horse two months later and again in Operation Thayer in October [H28]. Masher/White Wing is the template of the phase: a tactical success measured by body count, a large refugee population, and an enemy whose infrastructure in the hamlets survived intact.

## ◆ EV000-25 · The fall of the A Shau camp · 8–10 Mar 1966 · A Shau Special Forces camp, A Shau valley, Thua Thien Province · HIST · 000
The A Shau camp lay about 30 miles southwest of Hue and 2 km from the Laotian border, astride a main infiltration route into I Corps [H29]. It was garrisoned by ten Green Berets of the 5th Special Forces Group and about 210 CIDG, reinforced on 7 March by seven more Americans, nine interpreters and a MIKE Force company [H29]. Intelligence pointed to four battalions of the PAVN 325th Division, identified as the 95B Regiment [H29] [H22]. The assault came on 9 March under low cloud that kept most tactical air away and prevented reinforcement from Hue and Phu Bai [H29]. A-1 Skyraiders and AC-47 gunships flew below the overcast to support the defenders [H29].

By 10 March the camp had fallen. The Special Forces team lost five killed and twelve wounded; of a garrison of 434, 186 were evacuated by helicopter and the rest were listed as missing, a total accounted differently in every source [H29]. On 10 March Major Bernard F. Fisher landed his A-1E on the debris-strewn strip under fire to pick up Major D. W. Myers, who had crash-landed there, and received the Medal of Honor [H29]. The valley was not retaken. The PAVN made it a base area and a terminus of the Trail for the rest of the war, and US and ARVN forces never re-established a permanent presence there [H29].

## ◆ EV000-26 · The Buddhist uprising · 10 Mar – 19 Jun 1966 · Da Nang and Hue · HIST · 000
At the Honolulu conference in February 1966 Johnson embraced Ky publicly, and Ky came away believing he had American backing to move against his principal rival, Lieutenant General Nguyen Chanh Thi of I Corps [H30]. On 10 March the junta dismissed Thi [H30]. When Ky let him return to Da Nang and Hue on 16–17 March he was met by crowds, and the "Struggle Movement" of Buddhists, students and I Corps soldiers, led by Thich Tri Quang, took control of the two cities and called for civilian government [H30]. Ky's first attempt to reassert control, landing marines at Da Nang on 3–5 April, was blocked by I Corps troops and withdrawn [H30]; on 9 April US Marines interposed on a Da Nang bridge to stop a rebel convoy [H30].

On 15 May Ky airlifted marines and airborne battalions into Da Nang and took the city centre; the I Corps commander, General Ton That Dinh, fled to the US Marine headquarters, and III MAF found itself between two factions of its ally, preventing a bridge and an ammunition dump being blown and readying jets to intercept Vietnamese aircraft if Ky's air force struck the rebels [H30]. Thi agreed to go into exile at the end of May; on 26 May a funeral riot burned the US Information Service library [H30]. In June the Struggle supporters blocked Hue's streets with family altars until police removed them; Tri Quang was arrested and placed under house arrest in Saigon, and government control of Hue was restored by 19 June [H30]. About 150 people were killed and more than 700 wounded on both sides, including 23 Americans wounded [H30].

The uprising ended the Buddhist movement as an organised political force and confirmed Thieu and Ky in power [H30]. It also suspended operations in I Corps for three months at the height of the American buildup, and was answered with a political concession: elections for a Constituent Assembly, held on 11 September 1966 [H].

## ◆ EV000-27 · The POL strikes · 29 Jun 1966 · Hanoi and Haiphong petroleum storage areas · HIST · 000
On 28 June 1966, after weeks of postponement for weather and leaks, McNamara asked the President for authority to strike the two principal petroleum, oil and lubricant storage installations in the Hanoi–Haiphong area; Johnson, worried among other things about hitting a Soviet tanker in Haiphong harbour, assented, and the strikes went in on 29 June [H44]. McNamara's argument was that the North's ability to support the war in the South depended on its fuel [H44]. The strikes destroyed most of the bulk storage the North then had [H]. They did not affect its war effort: North Vietnam had already begun dispersing fuel into drums and small caches across the countryside, and imports through Haiphong continued [H]. By the autumn the intelligence community concluded that the POL campaign had not measurably reduced the flow of men and supplies to the South [H]. It was the most important target system Rolling Thunder was allowed to attack before 1967, and the clearest demonstration that an agrarian economy supplied by its allies could absorb strategic bombing directed at a modern economy's vulnerabilities.

## ◆ EV000-28 · Operation Hastings · 15 Jul – 3 Aug 1966 · Song Ngan valley, the Rockpile and Hill 208, Quang Tri Province, south of the DMZ · HIST · 000
In mid-1966 the PAVN 324B Division crossed the DMZ into Quang Tri Province in strength, treating the demilitarized zone as no barrier at all [H31]. The 3rd Marine Division under Major General Wood B. Kyle formed Task Force Delta under Brigadier General Lowell English, with the 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines, 1st Battalion, 3rd Marines, 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines and 3rd Battalion, 4th Marines, the 3rd Battalion, 12th Marines in support, and later the Special Landing Force battalion, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, from Operation Deckhouse II [H31]. The ARVN 1st Division under Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong ran Lam Son 289 alongside with an airborne task force [H31]. About 8,000 Americans and 3,000 ARVN faced 8,000–10,000 PAVN, including the 90th Regiment, about 1,500 men, and the 812th Regiment [H31].

The opening air assault into the Song Ngan valley on 15 July lost three CH-46s in a collision and another to fire, killing 13 Marines; the valley was named "Helicopter Valley" [H31]. On 18 July the 3rd Battalion, 4th Marines, pulling out of Landing Zone Crow, lost 14 dead and 49 wounded to a PAVN assault and counted 138 PAVN bodies [H31]. On 24 July the 6th Battalion, 812th Regiment hit Company I, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines on Hill 362, killing 18 and wounding 82 [H31]. The operation ended with 126 Americans and 21 South Vietnamese killed and about 700 PAVN claimed killed and 17 captured [H31]. It pushed the 324B Division back across the DMZ. Its lasting effect was to draw the Marines north: from 1966 to 1968 the 3rd Marine Division was built up along the DMZ, away from the coastal pacification on which III MAF had wanted to concentrate [H31].

## ◆ EV000-29 · The battle of Long Tan · 18 Aug 1966 · Long Tan rubber plantation near Nui Dat, Phuoc Tuy Province · HIST · 000
On the afternoon of 18 August 1966 D Company, 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 108 men under Major Harry Smith, sweeping east of the 1st Australian Task Force base at Nui Dat after a mortar attack the night before, met the VC 275th Regiment of the 5th Division and the provincial D445 Battalion, possibly with a PAVN battalion, in the Long Tan rubber plantation [H32]. Monsoon rain cut visibility to about 50 metres [H32]. For about three hours the company, scattered in platoons, held against repeated assaults with the support of the 1st Field Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, including the New Zealand 161st Battery, and the US A Battery, 2nd Battalion, 35th Artillery; two RAAF No. 9 Squadron UH-1Bs dropped ammunition through the rain; at dusk A Company, 6 RAR arrived in the M113s of 3 Troop, 1st APC Squadron under Lieutenant Adrian Roberts and the VC broke contact [H32].

Australian losses were 18 killed and 24 wounded [H32]. The Australians counted 245 enemy dead on the field in the following days and claimed 350 wounded and 3 captured; VC and PAVN sources give 47 killed and 100 wounded and about 700 men engaged, against Australian estimates of 1,500–2,500 [H32]. The truth lies somewhere between the two accounts, closer to the Australian body count than to the Vietnamese admission, since that count was of bodies found. The battle secured Nui Dat and gave the Task Force freedom of action in Phuoc Tuy for the rest of its tour.

## ◆ EV000-30 · Operation Attleboro · 14 Sep – 25 Nov 1966 · War Zone C, northwest of Dau Tieng, Tay Ninh and Binh Duong Provinces · HIST · 000
Attleboro began on 14 September 1966 as a brigade shakedown by the newly arrived 196th Light Infantry Brigade under Brigadier General Edward de Saussure, searching for caches northwest of Dau Tieng [H33]. In late October and early November it found more than it was looking for: the VC 9th Division, with its 271st, 272nd and 273rd Regiments and the PAVN 101st Regiment on loan from the 7th Division [H33]. The brigade, combing the jungle with rifle companies, was caught in a three-day fight that cost it 60 dead and 159 wounded [H33]. II Field Force, Vietnam took over and turned it into a corps operation: the 1st Infantry Division under Major General William E. DePuy assumed command, with the 25th Infantry Division under Major General Frederick C. Weyand, a brigade of the 4th Infantry Division and ARVN and Nung units [H33].

The operation cost the Americans 155 killed and 494 wounded [H33]. The US claimed 1,016 enemy dead; the PAVN admitted about half that, and an independent estimate gives about 500 [H33]. Some 127 individual and 19 crew-served weapons were captured; 843 tons of rice were uncovered early and more than 1,300 tons in six caches near Ben Cui [H33]. Captured documents later showed that DePuy had overestimated the damage: the 101st was badly hurt, the 271st and 272nd took moderate losses and the 273rd was untouched [H33]. Attleboro became the model for the multi-division search-and-destroy operations of 1967, and like them it left VC political control of the province intact once the Americans had gone [H33].

## ◆ EV000-31 · Operation Bolo · 2 Jan 1967 · Over the Hanoi area, North Vietnam · HIST · 000
By late 1966 the MiG-21s of the VPAF were attacking F-105 strike formations from bases the rules of engagement placed off limits. On 2 January 1967 the 8th Tactical Fighter Wing under Colonel Robin Olds flew F-4C Phantoms along the routes and at the altitudes and speeds of an F-105 strike, using F-105 call signs and electronic countermeasures pods [H] [H9]. The MiG-21s rose to meet what they took for bomb-laden Thunderchiefs, and seven were shot down in twelve minutes with no US loss [H9]. It was the most successful single air battle of Rolling Thunder for the United States, and it bought a few months' relief; the VPAF stood down to retrain and came back with better tactics, and its strength grew from about 100 interceptors in 1967 to 180 MiGs by 1968 [H9].

## ◆ EV000-32 · Operation Cedar Falls · 8–26 Jan 1967 · The Iron Triangle and Ben Suc, Binh Duong Province · HIST · 000
Cedar Falls attacked the Iron Triangle, the VC base area between the Saigon and Thi Tinh rivers about 40 km northwest of Saigon that held the headquarters of VC Military Region 4, the 272nd and 165th Regiments and the Phu Loi Local Force Battalion [H34]. On 8 January a battalion of the 1st Infantry Division air-assaulted into the village of Ben Suc; the 1st and 25th Infantry Divisions, the 196th Light Infantry Brigade, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment then sealed and searched the triangle with ARVN units, Rome plows clearing the jungle [H34] [H]. The whole population of Ben Suc and the surrounding hamlets, about 6,000 people, two-thirds of them children, was removed to a camp at Phu Loi and the village was destroyed; 106 were detained after screening [H34]. Infantry "tunnel rats" went into the tunnel complexes for the first time; 25 tunnels, about 100 bunkers and more than 500 structures were destroyed [H34].

The United States lost 72 killed and 337 wounded and the ARVN 11 killed and 8 wounded [H34]. The US claimed about 720–750 VC killed, 280 captured and 540 Chieu Hoi defectors, and captured rice enough to feed 13,000 men for a year [H34]. Within two days of the operation's end VC forces were back in the triangle, and within ten days a US report described it as "literally crawling" with them [H34]. A year later it was a staging area for the attack on Saigon at Tet [H34]. Cedar Falls embodies the phase's dilemma in the countryside: the population could be moved and the base destroyed, but a base area emptied of people was not held by anyone.

## ◆ EV000-33 · Operation Junction City · 22 Feb – 14 May 1967 · War Zone C, Tay Ninh Province, to the Cambodian border · HIST · 000
Junction City, under II Field Force (Lieutenant General Jonathan O. Seaman, then Lieutenant General Bruce Palmer from 18 March), sent the 1st and 25th Infantry Divisions, the 173rd Airborne Brigade, the 196th Light Infantry Brigade, the 3rd Brigade of the 4th Infantry Division and the 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment with ARVN forces into War Zone C to destroy the VC 9th Division and find COSVN, the Central Office for South Vietnam, which American analysts imagined as a fixed headquarters [H35]. On 22 February 845 men of the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry and Battery A, 3rd Battalion, 319th Artillery jumped from 13 C-130s near Katum, the only major US combat parachute assault of the war [H35] [H].

The enemy chose to fight several times, always at night or at dawn, against prepared positions: on 28 February the 101st Regiment hit a company of the 1st Division's 1st Brigade at Prek Klok and lost 167 dead to the Americans' 25 [H35]; on 10 March the 272nd Regiment attacked Fire Support Base II at Prek Klok and lost 197 to 3 [H35]; on 19 March the 273rd attacked Fire Support Base 20 at Ap Bau Bang and lost 227 to 3 [H35]; on 21 March the 272nd and U-80 Artillery assaulted Fire Support Base Gold at Suoi Tre and were broken by artillery firing beehive rounds at point-blank range and the arrival of armour, losing 647 dead to the Americans' 31 killed and 109 wounded [H35] [H]; and on 31 March the 273rd and a battalion of the 70th Guard Regiment attacked Landing Zone George at Ap Gu, losing about 600 to 17 [H35]. The operation used 366,000 artillery rounds and 3,235 tons of bombs [H35].

The United States lost 282 killed and 1,576 wounded and claimed 2,728 enemy killed [H35]. The Vietnamese Ministry of Defence gave 255 killed and 1,275 casualties in all in 2017, which is too low for the battles recorded [H35]. COSVN was not found; it moved, and the 9th Division withdrew its main forces into the Cambodian sanctuary, which expanded [H35]. Junction City showed that the VC would lose heavily when they attacked American firebases, and that they would decide for themselves whether to do so; after it, the enemy's main forces in III Corps fought from Cambodia, and the base area returned to VC control when the Americans left [H35].

## ◆ EV000-34 · The Hill Fights at Khe Sanh · 24 Apr – 11 May 1967 · Hills 861, 881 South and 881 North, northwest of Khe Sanh, Quang Tri Province · HIST · 000
On 24 April 1967 a Marine patrol from Khe Sanh ran into PAVN troops on Hill 861, setting off three weeks of fighting for the hills that dominate the Khe Sanh plateau [H41]. The PAVN 325C Division had six battalions on the hills, preparing the ground for an attack on the Khe Sanh base [H41]. The 2nd and 3rd Battalions, 3rd Marines, with companies of the 9th Marines, took the hills one at a time against bunkers built to survive bombing: 861 on 28 April after the PAVN withdrew, 881 South on 2 May, 881 North on 5 May, with B-52 strikes and heavy artillery fire [H41]. The new M16 rifles carried by the Marines jammed repeatedly in the fighting, and Marines were found dead beside rifles they had been trying to clear; the failures led to a congressional inquiry and changes in ammunition and maintenance [H].

The Marines lost 155 killed and 425 wounded and reported 940 PAVN killed [H41]. About 1,500 Marines had fought about 2,000 PAVN [H41]. The attack on Khe Sanh was forestalled for the year, and the hills were garrisoned. The fighting confirmed the PAVN's interest in the northwest corner of Quang Tri, and fixed Westmoreland's attention on it for the next nine months.

## ◆ EV000-35 · CORDS is established · 9 May 1967 · Saigon · HIST · 000
On 9 May 1967 the President placed the American pacification effort, civil and military, under MACV as Civil Operations and Revolutionary Development Support, with Robert W. Komer as one of Westmoreland's deputies, holding ambassadorial rank and authority over military personnel and resources, the first civilian to serve in such a role inside a US military command [H37]. It followed the failure of the Office of Civil Operations, set up in November 1966 to coordinate the civil agencies under civilian leadership [H37]. CORDS was about 85 percent military [H37]. Each corps had a CORDS deputy, usually civilian, under the corps senior adviser, and each province an American province senior adviser with civilian and military staffs alongside the Vietnamese province chief, usually an ARVN colonel [H37].

Komer's priorities were the territorial forces and the attack on the VC infrastructure. The Regional and Popular Forces numbered about 300,000 in 1967 [H37]; their advisory presence was later multiplied through Mobile Advisory Teams [H37]. In mid-1967 CORDS created the Intelligence Coordination and Exploitation programme, ICEX, to target the VCI, which became the Phoenix programme at the end of the year [H]. The Hamlet Evaluation System, introduced in January 1967, began rating every hamlet monthly on a scale reported by the American district advisers [H]; its figures were at once an indispensable record and a measure produced by officers rated on the result (A13). CORDS solved the American management problem of pacification. It did not solve the Vietnamese one, that security in the hamlet at night depended on Vietnamese forces and officials who had to stay there.

## ◆ EV000-36 · Operation Buffalo and the siege of Con Thien · 2 Jul – 31 Oct 1967 · Con Thien and "the Marketplace", Quang Tri Province, south of the DMZ · HIST · 000
Con Thien, a low hill 2 miles south of the DMZ and the western anchor of the planned strongpoint barrier, was the most exposed Marine position in the country, within range of PAVN artillery north of the Ben Hai [H42]. On 2 July 1967, at a place the Marines called the Marketplace, PAVN forces ambushed and nearly destroyed Company B, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines; it was the single worst day for the Marines in Vietnam, with 86 killed [H42]. The resulting Operation Buffalo, 2–14 July, cost 159 Marines killed and 345 wounded; US sources claimed 1,290 PAVN killed [H42]. In August there were 60 Arc Light strikes around the position [H42].

From September the PAVN laid Con Thien under siege by fire. Shelling ran at 200 rounds a day and more, rising to about 1,200 rounds on 25 September; between 19 and 27 September more than 3,000 rounds hit the base [H42]. The Marines called it "the Meat Grinder" [H42]. The answer was firepower: Operation Neutralize brought B-52s, tactical air and naval gunfire onto the PAVN artillery and assembly areas [H], with 12,577 Marine artillery rounds, 6,148 naval rounds and more than 5,200 Marine and USAF sorties [H42]. The siege lifted in October. Con Thien was held, but the Marines along the DMZ had become a static garrison under artillery they could not reach on the ground, because north of the Ben Hai was North Vietnam.

## ◆ EV000-37 · Hanoi decides on a general offensive · 6 Jul 1967 – Jan 1968 · Hanoi and COSVN · HIST · 000
In April 1967 COSVN under General Nguyen Chi Thanh proposed a decisive general offensive in the South, and in May sent the plan to Hanoi [H39]. Thanh briefed the Politburo in July and died there on 6 July, by the most common account of a heart attack after a party, by another of wounds from a US bombing raid [H39]. The plan was carried forward by the militants around Le Duan and Le Duc Tho; General Vo Nguyen Giap, who had favoured protracted war, did not originate it and modified it reluctantly [H39]. Beginning on 27 July, hundreds of moderates, officers and intellectuals were arrested in the "Revisionist Anti-Party Affair", with a second wave in November and December, which removed opposition to the offensive and much of Giap's staff [H39].

The premise was that the ARVN was no longer effective and the Saigon government unpopular, and that a general offensive in the cities would set off a general uprising [H39]. In October the Politburo chose the Tet holiday of 1968 as the date; it reaffirmed the decision in December and formalized it as Resolution 14 in January 1968 [H39]. The border battles of the autumn, at Con Thien, Loc Ninh, Song Be and Dak To, were part of the preparation, drawing US forces away from the cities [H36]. This was a decision taken in Hanoi for Hanoi's reasons: the stalemate in the South, the factional struggle in the Party and a reading of the South that proved wrong.

## ◆ EV000-38 · The constitution and the presidential election · 3 Sep 1967 · Republic of Vietnam · HIST · 000
The Constituent Assembly elected in September 1966 produced a constitution, promulgated on 1 April 1967 [H38]. In the presidential election of 3 September 1967, held with the Senate election, Thieu ran for president with Ky as his running mate, after the generals forced Ky to stand aside [H38]. Eleven tickets ran. Thieu and Ky won 34.83 percent, 1,649,561 votes; the runner-up, Truong Dinh Dzu, a lawyer campaigning on negotiations with the NLF, won 17.26 percent, 817,120 votes [H38]. The reported turnout was 83.17 percent of 5,853,251 registered voters [H38]. There were credible reports of soldiers showing voters how to mark their ballots, and of a secret military committee that would govern behind the elected government; on 10 August 57 members of the US House had condemned the conduct of the campaign [H38]. Dzu was later imprisoned [H]. Thieu was inaugurated on 31 October and the lower house was elected on 22 October [H] [H38].

The election gave the Republic of Vietnam an elected government for the first time since 1963 and, under Thieu, the stability that the previous four years had lacked. It did not give it legitimacy in the countryside: two-thirds of the voters chose someone else, and a civilian peace candidate had come second.

## ◆ EV000-39 · The barrier and Muscle Shoals · 8 Sep – Dec 1967 · The DMZ and the Laotian panhandle; Nakhon Phanom, Thailand · HIST · 000
In 1966 the Jason Division of the Institute for Defense Analyses, at McNamara's request, studied an anti-infiltration barrier of mines and sensors, and on 15 September 1966 McNamara placed Lieutenant General Alfred D. Starbird at the head of a Defense Communications Planning Group to build it [H43]. Johnson authorized construction on 13 January 1967 [H43]. Its eastern, conventional part, a cleared strip with strongpoints at Gio Linh, Con Thien and the bases west of them, was built under fire by the Marines in 1967; its western, electronic part across the Laotian panhandle was named Muscle Shoals on 8 September 1967 [H43] [H42]. Air-delivered seismic and acoustic sensors, the ADSID and the ACOUSID among them, developed in part from the Navy's sonobuoys, would be dropped by OP-2E Neptunes of the Navy's VO-67 squadron and relayed by EC-121R aircraft to an Infiltration Surveillance Center, Task Force Alpha, at Nakhon Phanom in Thailand, where IBM 360 computers analysed the signals [H43]. Field testing began in southeastern Laos on 25 November 1967 [H43]. Construction cost $1–1.7 billion and operation about $1 billion a year [H43]. The system, renamed Igloo White in 1968, would find trucks on the Trail at night as nothing before had; whether it reduced what arrived in the South is a question for later phases.

## ◆ EV000-40 · The battle of Dak To · 3–23 Nov 1967 · Dak To and Hills 1338, 724 and 875, Kontum Province · HIST · 000
In late October and early November 1967 the PAVN 1st Division, with its 24th, 32nd, 66th and 174th Regiments and the 40th Artillery Regiment, moved into the hills around Dak To near the tri-border with Laos and Cambodia, and a defector gave away much of its plan [H36]. The 4th Infantry Division and the 173rd Airborne Brigade, with the 1st, 2nd and 4th Battalions, 503rd Infantry, the 3rd Battalion, 12th Infantry, the 3rd Battalion, 8th Infantry and two battalions of the 1st Cavalry Division, and the ARVN 42nd Regiment and 2nd, 3rd and 9th Airborne Battalions, fought for the ridges in three weeks of bunker fighting in double- and triple-canopy jungle [H36]. The 3rd Battalion, 12th Infantry took Hill 1338 through a bunker complex linked by field telephone; on Hill 724 the PAVN struck the laager of the 3rd Battalion, 8th Infantry, killing 18 and wounding 118 [H36]. On 15 November mortar fire set off the ammunition dump at Dak To, destroying more than 1,100 tons of ordnance and two C-130s [H36].

From 19 to 23 November the 2nd and 4th Battalions, 503rd Infantry fought for Hill 875; on the first evening a misdirected US bomb fell on the 2nd Battalion's perimeter, killing many of its men [H36]. By the time the paratroopers took the crest on 23 November the PAVN had withdrawn [H36]. The Americans lost 361 killed, 15 missing and 1,441 wounded, and about 40 helicopters; the ARVN 73 killed [H36]. US figures for PAVN dead run from about 1,000 to 1,644, with allegations of inflation; a PAVN report gives about 450 killed and 1,089 wounded [H36]. The battle consumed 151,000 artillery rounds, 2,096 tactical air sorties, 257 B-52 strikes and 2,101 Army helicopter sorties [H36]. Westmoreland called it a defeat for the enemy. It was also exactly what Hanoi intended: one of the border battles that, with Loc Ninh, Song Be and Con Thien, drew US forces to the frontiers, so that by January 1968 about half the US manoeuvre battalions in South Vietnam were in the border regions [H36].

## How the phase ends
At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam [H40] and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year [H40]. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December [H9], and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December [H39]. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000 [H39], and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view" [H39]. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi [H]. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a low base.

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

---

# Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals of the South at once, breaking the Tet truce and every assumption of the American progress campaign. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no general uprising, the cities are retaken, Hue after a month, and the Viet Cong lose the larger part of the cadres and local forces they had built over a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes. Within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's request for 206,000 more men, halted most of the bombing of the North, offered negotiations and withdrawn from the presidential race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592 in the year, the highest of the war [H40], and US strength in Vietnam stands at about 537,000 at its end [H40].

The phase has three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, and three American responses. The first is military: Khe Sanh is held under the heaviest bombardment in the history of air warfare, the cities are cleared, and a new commander, General Creighton W. Abrams, takes over in June. The second is political: the decision of 31 March caps the American commitment and opens talks in Paris. The third is the countryside: with the VC's main and local forces weakened and its infrastructure exposed in the offensive, the government and CORDS move into the vacuum, with a general mobilization in June, the Phoenix programme and an Accelerated Pacification Campaign from November. The year ends with the bombing of the North stopped, a new president elected on a promise to end the war, and the war's centre of gravity shifting from the American divisions to the territorial forces and the hamlets.

The human cost in the South is the heaviest of the war to date. The offensive and the counter-attacks create about 630,000 new refugees, on top of about 800,000 displaced before; more than 70,000 homes are destroyed; by the end of the year about one South Vietnamese in twelve lives in a refugee camp [H39]. The government counts 14,300 civilian dead and 24,000 wounded in the first phase alone [H39].

## ◆ EV000-41 · The siege of Khe Sanh · 21 Jan – 15 Apr 1968 · Khe Sanh Combat Base, Lang Vei and the surrounding hills, Quang Tri Province · HIST · 000
In January 1968 the PAVN massed around the Marine base at Khe Sanh, in the northwest corner of Quang Tri Province astride Route 9 to Laos. The 304th and 325C Divisions were close in, with the 320th and 324th Divisions in the region [H46]. The base and its hill outposts were held by the 26th Marines under Colonel David E. Lownds, with the 1st Battalion, 9th Marines and other battalions, and from 27 January the ARVN 37th Ranger Battalion [H46]. The siege began on 21 January with an assault on Hill 861 and a bombardment that blew up the base's main ammunition dump [H]. Westmoreland, who expected Hanoi to attempt "Dien Bien Phu in reverse", answered with Operation Niagara: intelligence collection by sensors and reconnaissance, followed by a campaign in which about 60 B-52s attacked on an average day and more than 100,000 tons of bombs fell by mid-April, with more than 158,000 artillery rounds fired in the first three months [H46].

On 7 February twelve PT-76 amphibious tanks of the 203rd Armored Regiment, with infantry of the 304th Division, overran the Special Forces camp at Lang Vei, the first PAVN tank attack of the war; at least five tanks were knocked out, but of about 500 CIDG some 200 were killed or missing, and of 24 Americans ten were killed and eleven wounded [H46]. The base itself lived on air supply: about 14,356 tons came by air, 8,120 of them by parachute, much of it by C-130s using the Low Altitude Parachute Extraction System, and from late February the "Super Gaggle" of A-4s suppressing flak let helicopters supply the hill outposts [H46]. The air bridge cost a KC-130, three C-123s and 35 helicopters [H46].

Operation Pegasus, the 1st Cavalry Division's overland relief along Route 9, began on 1 April, linked up with the base on 8 April and ended on 15 April; it cost 92 Americans and 33 ARVN killed [H46]. Official US figures for the siege itself are more than 274 killed and 2,500 wounded; the PAVN acknowledged about 2,469 killed between January and July; US intelligence counted 1,602 bodies and estimated 10,000–15,000 dead, while a secret MACV report estimated 5,550 to the end of March [H46]. Whether Hanoi ever meant to take the base, or used it to fix American attention on the border while the cities were attacked, is disputed to this day; a captured PAVN study of 1974 said the PAVN would have taken it if it could, at a price it was not willing to pay [H46].

## ◆ EV000-42 · The Tet Offensive: the first wave · 30–31 Jan 1968 · Saigon, Hue and the provincial and district capitals of South Vietnam · HIST · 000
Shortly after midnight on 30 January, a day early because of a confusion in calendars, VC and PAVN forces attacked Nha Trang, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum, Hoi An, Tuy Hoa, Da Nang, Qui Nhon and Pleiku in I and II Corps [H39]. The warning was not fully heeded: half the ARVN was on holiday leave for Tet [H]. At 03:00 on 31 January the main wave struck Saigon, Cholon and Gia Dinh and the rest of the country [H39]. In all, between about 70,000 and 84,000 PAVN and VC troops attacked more than 100 towns and cities: 36 of the 44 provincial capitals, 5 of the 6 autonomous cities, between 64 and 72 of the 245 district towns, and the capital [H39].

The plan called for the general offensive to set off a general uprising of the urban population. None came. In most towns the attackers were driven out within days by the ARVN, whose units, against American and Vietnamese expectations, generally fought, and by US forces; in Saigon, Hue, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum, Can Tho and Ben Tre the fighting lasted longer and destroyed large parts of the towns [H]. The VC local forces and the urban cadres, who had surfaced to lead the uprising, were exposed and killed in large numbers. The United States claimed more than 45,000 PAVN and VC killed and 5,800 captured in the first phase, to 8 April, a figure even its own historians call excessively optimistic; Westmoreland gave 32,000 killed [H39]. Allied losses in the offensive were 2,788 ARVN killed, 8,299 wounded and 587 missing, and 1,536 US and other allied killed, 7,764 wounded and 11 missing [H39]. The PAVN official history gives communist casualties for the three phases of 1968 as 111,179, including 45,267 killed [H39].
