## ◆ EV000-43 · The battle for Saigon and the attack on the US embassy · 31 Jan – 7 Mar 1968 · Saigon, Cholon and Tan Son Nhut · HIST · 000
At 02:45 on 31 January a 19-man team of the VC C-10 Sapper Battalion blew a hole in the wall of the new US embassy compound in Saigon and fought inside the grounds for more than six hours without entering the chancery; the compound was secured by 09:20, and five Americans were killed [H39] [H]. The sappers were all killed or captured [H]. Other VC units attacked Tan Son Nhut air base with three battalions, the Joint General Staff compound, the Presidential Palace and the naval headquarters, and held the national radio station for about six hours, though they could not broadcast [H39]. The image of the embassy under attack, broadcast in the United States hours after Westmoreland had declared the enemy's offensive capacity broken, did more political damage than any battle of the war [H].

The fighting in Saigon lasted weeks in Cholon, the Chinese quarter, where VC battalions held out around the Phu Tho racetrack. On 4 February residents were ordered out and the area declared a free-fire zone; the last battle in Cholon was fought on 7 March [H39]. On 1 February the national police chief, Brigadier General Nguyen Ngoc Loan, shot a captured VC officer in the head in a Saigon street before a photographer and a film camera [H]. The image became, with the embassy, the American public's picture of Tet.

## ◆ EV000-44 · The battle of Hue · 31 Jan – 2 Mar 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · HIST · 000
In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments with the 1st, 2nd and 12th Sapper Battalions, under a Hue City Front command, took almost all of Hue, the old imperial capital, except the ARVN 1st Division headquarters in the northeast corner of the Citadel and the MACV advisory compound south of the Perfume River [H45]. Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong held his headquarters with his staff and the Hac Bao Reconnaissance Company, and brought in the 3rd Regiment, the 4th Battalion, 2nd Regiment, the 1st Airborne Task Force (2nd and 7th Airborne Battalions), Vietnamese Marine Task Force A, the 7th Armored Cavalry Squadron and the 21st and 39th Ranger Battalions [H45]. The PAVN reinforced with the 7th Battalion, 29th Regiment of the 325C Division from Khe Sanh, the 803rd Regiment and a battalion of the 90th Regiment of the 324B Division, and the 6th Battalion, 24th Regiment of the 304th Division [H45].

South of the river the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines and the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 5th Marines of Task Force X-Ray cleared the new city block by block, house by house, in rain and low cloud that restricted air support for most of the battle [H45] [H]. Outside the city the 3rd Brigade of the 1st Cavalry Division, with the 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry, the 5th Battalion, 7th Cavalry and the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry, fought to cut the PAVN routes in from the west and did not reach the Citadel's west wall until 25 February [H45]. The ARVN and the Marines retook the Citadel; the flag of the Front came down from its tower on 24 February, and the battle was declared over on 2 March [H].

The ARVN lost 458 killed and about 2,700 wounded, and the Americans 250 killed and 1,554 wounded [H45]. PAVN and VC dead are given from 1,042 to more than 5,000, by source [H45]. Between 5,800 and 8,000 civilians died and the city was largely destroyed [H45]. During their occupation the PAVN and VC rounded up officials, officers, priests, teachers, foreigners and others on prepared lists; after the battle mass graves were found, and more than 2,000 people are known to have been executed, with the most cited count of bodies recovered at about 2,800 [H45] [H]. Hue was the only city the offensive held for more than a few days, and the killings there hardened the urban population of the South against the Front for the rest of the war.

## ◆ EV000-45 · The reinforcement request and the decision of 31 March · 20 Feb – 31 Mar 1968 · Saigon and Washington · HIST · 000
On 12 February Westmoreland asked for 10,500 more troops; on 13 February a brigade of the 82nd Airborne Division and a Marine regimental landing team, already authorized, were sent [H39] [H]. On 20 February the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Earle Wheeler, went to Saigon, and returned with a request for 206,000 more men, framed by the Chiefs to force a mobilization of the reserves [H]. On 28 February McNamara left office and on 1 March Clark Clifford succeeded him, charged with reviewing the request [H39] [H]. On 10 March the *New York Times* reported it [H]. On 12 March Senator Eugene McCarthy, running against the war, took 42 percent of the vote in the New Hampshire primary; on 16 March Senator Robert F. Kennedy entered the race [H]. On 25–26 March the senior outside advisers, the "Wise Men", told the President that the war could not be won at an acceptable cost [H].

On 31 March Johnson announced in a televised address that he was stopping the bombing of North Vietnam except in the area just north of the DMZ, that he would send only about 13,500 more troops, that the United States was ready to talk, and that he would not seek or accept his party's nomination for another term [H] [H9]. The speech capped the American commitment. Westmoreland's strategy of attrition by American forces had been judged by the President's own advisers to have no end that the country would accept, and from this point the questions were how to get out, and how to leave the South able to stand.

## ◆ EV000-46 · The My Lai massacre · 16 Mar 1968 · Son My village (My Lai 4 and My Khe), Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province · HIST · 000
On the morning of 16 March 1968 Company C, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry, 11th Brigade, Americal Division, operating under Task Force Barker, was landed by helicopter at the hamlet of My Lai 4 in Son My village, in an area of Quang Ngai long held by the VC 48th Local Force Battalion [H47] [H]. It met no resistance. Its men, led among others by Second Lieutenant William L. Calley, killed the unarmed villagers they found, mostly old men, women and children, in their homes, on the paths and in an irrigation ditch; Company B, 4th Battalion, 3rd Infantry killed civilians at My Khe nearby [H47]. The dead number from 347, the US Army figure, to 504, the Vietnamese figure [H47]. Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson, flying an OH-23 scout helicopter overhead, landed between the soldiers and a group of villagers, threatened to fire on his own side, and evacuated survivors; his crewman Glenn Andreotta pulled a wounded child from the ditch [H47].

The Army reported the operation as a victory over 128 Viet Cong, and the brigade's investigation conceded about 20 accidental civilian deaths [H47]. The cover-up held for a year and a half, until Ronald Ridenhour's letters to Congress in March 1969 and Seymour Hersh's report of 13 November 1969 [H47]. My Lai belongs to this phase as an event of the war in the countryside: a company of a division assembled hastily, under a command climate that measured success by bodies, in a province where the population was treated as the enemy's. Its effect on the war came later, when it became known.

## ◆ EV000-47 · The battle of Dai Do · 30 Apr – 3 May 1968 · Dai Do and the hamlets north of Dong Ha on the Cua Viet, Quang Tri Province · HIST · 000
At the end of April, as the second wave of the offensive began, battalions of the PAVN 320th Division, two of them identified as belonging to the 48th and 52nd Regiments, moved into the hamlets of Dai Do, Dinh To and their neighbours north of Dong Ha, threatening the Marine base and the Cua Viet supply route [H49]. The 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines under Lieutenant Colonel William Weise attacked across open paddies from amphibian tractors and boats, with the 1st Battalion, 3rd Marines, ARVN units of the 2nd Regiment and a mechanized battalion, and from 1 May the US 3rd Battalion, 21st Infantry [H49]. The Marines lost 81 killed and the ARVN 5; the Americans claimed more than 600 PAVN killed, and the PAVN has not released its losses [H49]. By 3 May the PAVN had gone. Whether Dai Do was a main thrust against Dong Ha or a diversion is not settled; the frontal assaults of 1 and 2 May were costly enough to be criticized by later historians [H49].

## ◆ EV000-48 · The Paris talks open · May 1968 · Paris · HIST · 000
After weeks of argument over a site, talks between the United States and North Vietnam opened in Paris in May 1968, with W. Averell Harriman leading for the United States and Xuan Thuy for Hanoi [H51]. They stalled at once: Hanoi demanded a complete and unconditional end to the bombing of the North before substantive talks, and refused to recognise the Saigon government; Saigon refused to sit with the Front [H51]. Through the summer the talks were a forum for statements, while both sides fought for position on the ground. Their opening nonetheless changed the war's logic. From May 1968 both governments were fighting to shape a settlement as well as to win, and every offensive that followed had a negotiating purpose.

## ◆ EV000-49 · The May offensive in Saigon · 5 May – 15 Jun 1968 · Saigon and its outskirts, and towns throughout the South · HIST · 000
On 5 May the PAVN and VC launched the second phase of the general offensive, which the Americans called "mini-Tet", with attacks by fire on more than 100 towns and installations and a renewed assault on Saigon [H39] [H]. VC battalions fought their way into the southern and western districts of the capital and into Cholon, where they were destroyed or driven out by the ARVN and US forces over several weeks, with air strikes and artillery used inside the city; much of District 8 was destroyed and tens of thousands were made homeless [H]. The phase lasted until 15 June [H39]. Its losses fell heavily on the same local forces and cadres who had survived February, and many of the units that fought in Saigon in May were filled out with northern replacements [H]. American deaths in May 1968 were the highest of any month of the war [H].

## ◆ EV000-50 · The evacuation of Kham Duc · 10–12 May 1968 · Kham Duc Special Forces camp and Ngok Tavak, Quang Tin Province · HIST · 000
On 10 May the 40th Battalion of the PAVN 2nd Division's 1st Regiment overran the outpost of Ngok Tavak, held by an Australian-led company of the 11th MIKE Force and a battery of the 2nd Battalion, 13th Marines [H48]. The PAVN 1st and 21st Regiments then closed on the camp at Kham Duc, held by Special Forces Detachment A-105, CIDG and a SOG detachment, reinforced by the 2nd Battalion, 1st Infantry of the Americal Division [H48]. On 11 May Westmoreland approved evacuation, and on 12 May, under about 350 air sorties, roughly 1,500 soldiers and civilians were flown out [H48]. A C-130 flown by Major Bernard L. Bucher was shot down just after take-off, killing all 183 Vietnamese civilians aboard, a Special Forces officer and the five crewmen; a second C-130 was wrecked on the runway [H48]. Lieutenant Colonel Joe M. Jackson landed a C-123 on the abandoned strip to recover a three-man combat control team left behind, and received the Medal of Honor [H48]. The Americans lost about 42–46 killed and 31–33 missing and twelve aircraft; about 220 CIDG were killed or missing; the US claimed about 345 PAVN killed, and a later study estimates 1,500–2,000 [H48]. The abandonment of the camp removed one of the few allied positions between the Laotian border and the lowlands of Quang Tin and Quang Nam, and its loss was one of the few clear PAVN victories over a US-defended position in 1968 [H48].

## ◆ EV000-51 · Abrams takes command; mobilization in the South; Khe Sanh abandoned · 10 Jun – 11 Jul 1968 · Saigon and Quang Tri Province · HIST · 000
On 10 June 1968 General Creighton W. Abrams, Westmoreland's deputy since May 1967, succeeded him as COMUSMACV; Westmoreland went home to be Army Chief of Staff [H50] [H]. Abrams spoke of "one war", in which the main-force battle, pacification and the improvement of the RVNAF were parts of one campaign rather than separate efforts, and gave more weight to the enemy's logistics system, to territorial security and to the South Vietnamese forces [H50]. How much changed in practice is disputed: large operations continued into 1969 and his own strategy papers did not announce a new strategy [H50].

In mid-June the National Assembly in Saigon passed the general mobilization law the government had been unable to pass before Tet, inducting men aged 18 to 38 and ordering youths of 17 and men of 39 to 43 into civil defence; about 220,000 men were inducted before the summer ended [H62]. RVNAF strength rose from about 643,000 in 1967 to about 897,000 in 1969 [H62]. On 19 June the Marines began evacuating Khe Sanh, which Westmoreland had held through the siege; the base was closed on 5 July and the last Marines left the area on 11 July [H46]. The decision was explained as the product of more helicopters and a mobile defence of the DMZ, but it was read by both sides as an admission of what the base had cost.

## ◆ EV000-52 · The third offensive · 17 Aug – 23 Sep 1968 · Provincial towns and bases, especially in III Corps and the Central Highlands · HIST · 000
The third phase of the general offensive began in mid-August with attacks by fire and ground assaults on towns and bases, including attacks around Tay Ninh in III Corps [H39] [H]. It was weaker than its predecessors: the local forces that had carried the attacks of February and May were largely gone, and the main forces would not commit themselves against American firepower in the same way again [H39]. It ended in late September without lasting gains [H39]. Taken together, the three offensives of 1968 cost the VC about 50,000 dead by one estimate against about 4,000 US and 6,000 ARVN [H39]. Their recruitment in the South collapsed: in Region 5, 1,700 recruits in 1969 against 8,000 in 1968, in the Mekong lowlands 100 against 16,000 [H39]. By the end of the year about 70 percent of the main-force troops in the South are reported to have been northerners [H39]. MACV estimated total PAVN and VC strength at 287,000 in January 1968 and 251,000 at its end [H39]. The losses forced a reassessment in Hanoi that would carry into 1969 [H].

## ◆ EV000-53 · The bombing halt and the American election · 31 Oct – 5 Nov 1968 · Washington, Paris and Saigon · HIST · 000
In October Hanoi signalled that it would accept the Saigon government at the table if the bombing stopped [H]. On 31 October Johnson announced the end of all bombing of North Vietnam from 1 November, ending Rolling Thunder [H9] [H51]. Thieu refused to join the talks on the terms agreed [H51]. Through Anna Chennault the Nixon campaign had encouraged him to wait for a better deal, and on 2 November she told the South Vietnamese ambassador to "hold on a while longer"; Johnson learned of it through intercepts and ordered the campaign watched, but did not make it public [H51]. Historians disagree on whether the channel changed anything, since Thieu had his own reasons to refuse [H51]. On 5 November Richard M. Nixon was elected president by a narrow popular margin [H]. Talks in Paris did not resume in substance until the new year, after a dispute over the shape of the table was settled with a round table for the governments [H51].

Over three years and eight months Rolling Thunder had flown 153,784 USAF and 152,399 Navy and Marine attack sorties [H9], and lost 506 USAF, 397 Navy and 19 Marine aircraft over or near the North [H9]. It ended without having achieved its purposes of breaking Hanoi's will or stopping the flow of men and supplies south.

## ◆ EV000-54 · The Accelerated Pacification Campaign and Phoenix · 1 Nov 1968 – Jan 1969 · The countryside of South Vietnam · HIST · 000
Phung Hoang, the Vietnamese programme to coordinate the attack on the VC infrastructure, had been established by decree in December 1967 out of the American ICEX programme of June 1967, and Thieu put his own decree behind it in July 1968 [H52]. Its instruments were district intelligence centres, the CIA-run Provincial Reconnaissance Units and the police; its method was to identify, capture, turn or kill the cadres of the parallel administration [H52]. On 1 November 1968, at the urging of Komer and his successor William E. Colby, the government launched the Accelerated Pacification Campaign, a three-month drive to raise about 1,000 contested hamlets to relative security before any ceasefire could freeze the map, using RF and PF, Revolutionary Development cadre and the new People's Self-Defence Force, with regular forces screening [H].

The campaign met its targets by the Hamlet Evaluation System, a scale filled in by American district advisers under pressure to show progress (A13), and in many places those hamlets did become more secure after dark, because the VC local forces that had protected the infrastructure had died in the offensives [H]. Phoenix's own figures, 81,740 people "neutralized" between 1968 and 1972, 26,369 of them killed, were produced against monthly quotas that encouraged false arrests and padding, and about 87 percent of the killings credited to it were by ordinary military operations [H52]. Communist cadres later described 1968–72 as their hardest period, and some American advisers concluded that Phoenix had been a mortal threat in some provinces and a paper programme in others [H52].

## ◆ EV000-55 · Commando Hunt begins · 15 Nov 1968 · The Laotian panhandle · HIST · 000
On 15 November, two weeks after the bombing of the North stopped, the Seventh Air Force opened Commando Hunt, a campaign against the Trail in southern Laos fought in seasonal phases: dry-season phases against the trucks moving south, wet-season phases against the roads [H53]. Aircraft freed from the North were moved to it. It was the first campaign built around Igloo White: sensors seeded along the roads reported to the Infiltration Surveillance Center at Nakhon Phanom, whose computers passed target coordinates to strike aircraft, and gunships, above all the AC-130 Spectre, hunted trucks at night [H53]. Phase I, to 20 April 1969, claimed 7,322 trucks destroyed at a cost of 56 allied aircraft to an estimated 600 anti-aircraft weapons [H53]. The truck counts were not believed by the CIA, which estimated the North's entire truck inventory at about 6,000 [H53]. Commando Hunt would run until March 1972, and the Trail would grow under it.

## How the phase ends
At the end of 1968 the war has changed shape without changing direction. The VC in the South have lost much of their main and local forces and many of their cadres in the three offensives, and their recruitment has collapsed; the main-force war is now predominantly a PAVN war, and the parallel administration in the hamlets, though intact in much of the country, is under more pressure than at any time since 1959. The government in Saigon has survived Tet, mobilized, and begun with CORDS to push into the countryside; ARVN units fought better in February than anyone expected, though they remain dependent on American firepower and logistics. Against these gains, the United States has decided not to escalate further and to seek a negotiated way out; the bombing of the North has ended; and the American public's tolerance for casualties, measured in a year in which 14,592 Americans died by hostile action, has been spent [H40].

In Hanoi, the leadership has paid heavily for the General Offensive and turned back to protracted war for the moment, but has won what it most needed: an American president who will not reinforce and a successor committed to withdrawal. The Paris talks exist; the shape of the table is being settled. Phase IV opens with a new administration in Washington, a war in the countryside that the South is better placed to fight than it has been for years, and an American army whose withdrawal is now a matter of timing.

---

# Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

Phase IV is the war of the American withdrawal. US strength peaks at about 539,000 in the first half of 1969 and falls to 474,000 at the end of that year, 336,000 at the end of 1970 and 158,000 at the end of 1971 [H40]. American deaths by hostile action fall with it, from about 9,414 in 1969 [D] to 4,221 in 1970 and 1,380 in 1971 [H40]. The Republic of Vietnam's armed forces grow to replace them: from about 897,000 in 1969 to 968,000 in 1970 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72, the territorial Regional and Popular Forces growing fastest [H62]. The policy has a name, Vietnamization, and a premise: that the South, given equipment, time and American air power, can hold what the Americans leave.

The shape of the phase is a race between the withdrawal and the South's improvement, run while Hanoi rebuilds. In the countryside, the years 1969–71 are the best the government ever has. The VC, gutted by the 1968 offensives, return to protracted war on a reduced scale; pacification spreads under Phoenix, the territorial forces and the Land to the Tiller reform; and by most indicators, including the ones the enemy cannot fake, the VC's hold on the population of the Delta and the coastal lowlands weakens. On the frontiers the war goes the other way. The North rebuilds its main forces, extends the Trail and its pipeline, and after Sihanouk's fall loses Sihanoukville but gains much of eastern Cambodia. The United States uses the time it has to strike the sanctuaries it had left alone, secretly from the air over Cambodia from March 1969, on the ground in Cambodia in May–June 1970, and through the ARVN alone in Laos in February–March 1971, and Congress closes the ground option behind each attempt.

At home the war's support is gone. The revelation of My Lai, the Moratorium, the Cambodian incursion and Kent State, the trial of Calley and the publication of the Pentagon Papers mark a country that wants its army home, and an army in Vietnam, after 1969, that is itself coming apart under drugs, racial conflict and attacks on its own officers, waiting to leave a war it no longer expects to win [H]. In Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh dies in September 1969; the collective leadership around Le Duan negotiates secretly with Kissinger and, after the ARVN's defeat in Laos in 1971, decides to try once more for victory by conventional invasion.

## ◆ EV000-56 · Nixon takes office; Vietnamization · 20 Jan – Mar 1969 · Washington and Saigon · HIST · 000
Richard Nixon was inaugurated on 20 January 1969 with a promise to end the war with honour and no published plan to do it [H]. His national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, commissioned a survey of the agencies' views of the war, which showed deep disagreement about almost everything except that the South could not yet stand alone [H]. At a National Security Council meeting on 28 January the Secretary of Defense, Melvin Laird, proposed calling the policy "Vietnamizing" the war; its two parts were to strengthen the RVNAF to take over the fighting and to extend pacification [H58]. Henry Cabot Lodge replaced Harriman in Paris [H51]. Laird, who visited Saigon in March, pressed for withdrawals sooner and larger than the military wanted, and made "Vietnamization" the measure of the South's progress [H] [H58]. The Improvement and Modernization programme behind it re-equipped the RVNAF from top to bottom: M16 rifles for the regulars and then the territorial forces, M60 machine guns, artillery, helicopters, aircraft, and the training base to use them [H].

## ◆ EV000-57 · The post-Tet offensive · 23 Feb – Mar 1969 · Saigon, Da Nang and installations throughout the South · HIST · 000
On the night of 22–23 February 1969 the PAVN and VC opened a countrywide offensive of attacks by fire and sapper raids against more than a hundred targets, including Saigon, Da Nang, Hue and US bases, the heaviest since 1968 [H]. It was smaller in scale and ambition than Tet: the ground attacks were mainly against bases and firebases, not into the cities, and the population did not rise [H]. It cost the Americans heavily in the first weeks, and it was taken in Washington as a breach of the understanding that had accompanied the bombing halt [H]. Nixon's answer, in the third week of March, was the secret bombing of the Cambodian base areas [H57].

## ◆ EV000-58 · Operation Menu · 18 Mar 1969 – 26 May 1970 · Base Areas 350, 351, 352, 353, 609 and 740, eastern Cambodia · HIST · 000
On the night of 18 March 1969, 60 B-52s took off from Guam on a mission ostensibly against targets in South Vietnam; 48 were diverted into Cambodia against Base Area 353 in the Fishhook, where COSVN was believed to be, and dropped about 2,400 tons that night [H57]. The campaign that followed, codenamed Breakfast, Lunch, Snack, Dinner, Supper and Dessert after the base areas it struck, flew about 3,800 B-52 sorties and dropped 108,823 tons until 26 May 1970 [H57]. It was concealed by dual reporting: an overt channel ordered strikes near the border inside South Vietnam, while a back channel ordered the strikes in Cambodia, whose records were destroyed after each mission; neither the Secretary of the Air Force nor its chief of staff was told [H57].

Sihanouk, whose territory it was and whose government had tolerated the base areas and the supply line from Sihanoukville, did not protest publicly [H]. The *New York Times* reported the bombing on 9 May 1969; Nixon ordered the leak traced, and the telephones of 13 officials and four journalists were tapped, the first of the abuses that led to Watergate [H57]. The bombing forced the PAVN and VC to disperse and camouflage their Cambodian bases but did not stop their offensives, and its effect on the war in the South is disputed [H57].

## ◆ EV000-59 · Hamburger Hill · 13–20 May 1969 · Ap Bia Mountain (Hill 937), A Shau valley, Thua Thien Province · HIST · 000
In May 1969 the 3rd Brigade of the 101st Airborne Division (Airmobile), under the division commander Major General Melvin Zais, went into the A Shau valley in Operation Apache Snow to destroy the PAVN base areas there [H54]. On Ap Bia Mountain, Hill 937, about 1.9 km from the Laotian border, the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry under Lieutenant Colonel Weldon Honeycutt met the 7th and 8th Battalions of the PAVN 29th Regiment, dug in [H54]. Ten days of frontal assaults followed, with the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry, the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry and the ARVN 2nd Battalion, 3rd Regiment joining for the final attack on 20 May [H54]. The Americans lost 56 killed, 367 wounded and 7 missing; they counted 630 PAVN dead on and around the hill, many in tunnels, and captured 89 individual and 22 crew-served weapons and 3 prisoners [H54]. On 5 June the hill was abandoned [H54].

"That hill had no military value whatsoever," Zais said [H54]. Senators Edward Kennedy, George McGovern and Stephen Young attacked the battle as senseless; on 27 June *Life* published the photographs of 242 Americans killed in one week [H54]. Abrams turned from "maximum pressure" to a posture designed to keep American casualties down, and Nixon announced the first troop withdrawal within weeks [H54].

## ◆ EV000-60 · Midway, the first withdrawals and the Nixon Doctrine · 8 Jun – Dec 1969 · Midway Island; Guam; South Vietnam · HIST · 000
On 8 June 1969 Nixon met Thieu on Midway Island and announced the first withdrawal of US troops, 25,000 men, to be completed by the end of August [H]. Elements of the 9th Infantry Division left the Mekong Delta in July, and the whole 3rd Marine Division had left I Corps by the end of the year [H] [H58]. On 25 July, at Guam, Nixon set out what became the Nixon Doctrine: the United States would honour its treaty commitments and provide a nuclear shield, but would look to its Asian allies to provide the manpower for their own defence [H]. Further withdrawals were announced in September and December [H]. For the troops still in Vietnam, the withdrawals made every American death harder to justify. Discipline in the US Army declined through 1969–71; drug use, racial violence and "fragging", attacks on officers and NCOs with grenades, became endemic in rear areas and in some combat units [H]. The withdrawals were faster than the RVNAF's improvement, and they ran on a timetable set by American politics, not by the war.

## ◆ EV000-61 · COSVN Resolution 9 and the death of Ho Chi Minh · Jul – 2 Sep 1969 · COSVN headquarters and Hanoi · HIST · 000
In July 1969 COSVN issued Resolution 9, which accepted that the 1968 offensives had not produced the uprising and directed a return to protracted war: small-unit and sapper attacks, economy of force, the rebuilding of the infrastructure, and a campaign against Vietnamization and pacification, while main forces were preserved in the sanctuaries [H]. It was a decision taken in the light of losses and on the movement's own reading of its position, and it set the pattern of the enemy's war in the South until 1971. On 2 September 1969 Ho Chi Minh died in Hanoi [H]. His testament called for the war to continue until the Americans had left and the country was reunified [H]. Power passed to a collective leadership in which Le Duan, as First Secretary, was the strongest figure, with Le Duc Tho, Truong Chinh and Pham Van Dong [H]. Ho's death did not change the policy; it removed the one figure whose authority stood above the factions, and left the militants who had planned Tet in charge.

## ◆ EV000-62 · The secret Paris channel opens · 4 Aug 1969 – Feb 1970 · Paris · HIST · 000
In June 1969 the National Liberation Front formed the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam, to claim governmental status at the talks [H51] [H]. On 4 August Kissinger began secret talks in Paris with Hanoi's delegation, first with Xuan Thuy, and from February 1970 with Le Duc Tho, a member of the Politburo [H51] [H]. The formal sessions at the Hotel Majestic became a forum for public statements; the substance moved to the secret channel. The core issues were fixed from the start and remained so for three years: Hanoi demanded the withdrawal of all US forces and the removal of Thieu as the price of a settlement, and would not discuss the withdrawal of its own forces from the South; Washington would not overthrow its ally [H51].

## ◆ EV000-63 · My Lai revealed; the Moratorium · 15 Oct – 24 Nov 1969 · Washington and the United States · HIST · 000
On 15 October 1969 the Moratorium brought hundreds of thousands of Americans out against the war in cities across the country, and on 15 November the Mobilization brought a march of several hundred thousand to Washington [H]. On 3 November Nixon appealed on television to "the great silent majority" to support his policy of withdrawal on his terms, and the speech was well received [H]. On 13 November Seymour Hersh published the story of the My Lai massacre, and on 20 November the photographs taken by the Army photographer Ronald Haeberle appeared [H47]. On 24 November the Army appointed Lieutenant General William Peers to investigate the cover-up; his report of 17 March 1970 found that at least 175–200 Vietnamese had been killed and condemned the concealment [H47]. My Lai became, in American opinion, the symbol of the war in the countryside, and in South Vietnam a weapon for the Front's propaganda in a province that had suffered it.

## ◆ EV000-64 · Sihanouk falls; the PAVN turns on Cambodia · 18 Mar – Apr 1970 · Phnom Penh and eastern Cambodia · HIST · 000
On 18 March 1970, while Sihanouk was abroad, the Cambodian National Assembly deposed him, and General Lon Nol became the head of a government hostile to the Vietnamese communists [H55]. Lon Nol closed the port of Sihanoukville to the supplies that had reached the PAVN and VC base areas through it [H55]. From 29 March the PAVN attacked the Cambodian army and within weeks overran much of eastern and northeastern Cambodia, protecting its bases and opening the country to the Khmer Rouge, whom it armed and trained [H55]. Cambodia, a sanctuary since 1965, became a battlefield. The loss of Sihanoukville threw the whole burden of supplying the southern half of South Vietnam onto the Trail, which in turn was extended through Laos and northeastern Cambodia.

## ◆ EV000-65 · Land to the Tiller · 26 Mar 1970 · Republic of Vietnam · HIST · 000
On 26 March 1970 Thieu signed the Land to the Tiller law [H63]. It limited individual holdings of rice land to 15 hectares, expropriated tenanted land beyond what the owner farmed himself, and gave it to the tenants who tilled it, with compensation to the landlords; the United States financed 339 million of the 441 million dollars it cost [H63]. Crucially, it confirmed title for peasants who had received land from the Viet Cong [H63]. It was more successful than any earlier land programme in the South, and it was aimed at one of the Front's strongest appeals in the Delta, the promise of land [H63] [H]. Historians debate whether it came "too little, too late" to change the war [H63]; its effects accrued over years, in the attitudes of the rural population towards a government that had for the first time given them something.

## ◆ EV000-66 · The Cambodian incursion · 29 Apr – 30 Jun 1970 · The Parrot's Beak and the Fishhook, eastern Cambodia · HIST · 000
On 29 April 1970 ARVN forces of III and IV Corps under Lieutenant General Do Cao Tri attacked into the Parrot's Beak west of Saigon, and on 1 May the US 1st Cavalry Division and 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, with ARVN airborne units, attacked into the Fishhook north of it; the 25th and 4th Infantry Divisions followed [H55]. Nixon announced it on television on 30 April as an attack on COSVN [H] [H55]. COSVN had moved before the attack [H55]. The PAVN and VC mostly avoided battle, leaving rearguards, and withdrew westward [H55]. In the base areas the allies found the logistics of the war in the South: about 22,900 individual and 2,500 crew-served weapons, 7,000–8,000 tons of rice, about 1,800 tons of ammunition, 431 vehicles and 55 tons of medical supplies [H55]. The allies claimed 11,369 PAVN and VC killed and 2,509 captured [H55]. US forces were out by 30 June; the ARVN stayed on [H55].

On 4 May Ohio National Guardsmen shot dead four students at Kent State University, and protests closed hundreds of campuses [H55] [H]. On 30 June the Senate passed the Cooper–Church amendment barring US ground forces from Cambodia [H55]. The incursion bought time: the loss of the caches and of Sihanoukville delayed the PAVN's recovery in III and IV Corps, and the southern half of the country was quieter for more than a year. It did not destroy the sanctuary. The PAVN rebuilt its supply routes, seized Attapeu and Saravane in Laos, opened a "Liberation Route" through northeastern Cambodia to the Mekong, and in 1972 would attack An Loc from Cambodia [H55].

## ◆ EV000-67 · Fire Support Base Ripcord · 1–23 Jul 1970 · Fire Support Base Ripcord, near the A Shau valley, Thua Thien Province · HIST · 000
In the spring of 1970 the 101st Airborne Division reopened Fire Support Base Ripcord on the eastern edge of the A Shau valley for an offensive against the PAVN base areas [H61]. From 1 July the PAVN 324B Division, with its 803rd Regiment at Ripcord, its 29th Regiment on the nearby hills and a battalion of the 6th Regiment of the Tri-Thien command in support, besieged the base, held by the 2nd Battalion, 506th Infantry of the 3rd Brigade under Colonel Ben Harrison [H61]. On 18 July a CH-47 hit by small-arms fire crashed into the ammunition storage area, killing four and destroying six M102 howitzers and 2,238 rounds of 105mm ammunition [H61]. The command judged the base indefensible and evacuated it on 23 July under fire; the battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Andre Lucas, was among the last killed and received the Medal of Honor posthumously [H61]. The Americans lost 75 killed and claimed 422 PAVN dead [H61]. It was the last major battle between US ground forces and the PAVN [H61]. Whether it crippled the PAVN in the region, as Harrison believed, or achieved the PAVN's purpose by forcing the Americans out, is disputed [H61].

## ◆ EV000-68 · Commando Hunt and the growth of the Trail · 10 Oct 1970 – Dec 1971 · The Laotian panhandle and northeastern Cambodia · HIST · 000
The dry-season phases of Commando Hunt were the main US effort against the North's logistics after 1968 [H53]. Phase V, from 10 October 1970 to 30 April 1971, claimed 16,266 trucks destroyed, a figure Seventh Air Force itself lowered to 11,000; in Phase VII the AC-130E gunships were credited with 7,335 of 10,689 trucks claimed [H53]. The CIA estimated that the entire North Vietnamese truck inventory was about 6,000, and a Defense Intelligence Agency model reached zero trucks remaining fourteen times in 1969 [H53]. Over the campaign the Air Force claimed 51,000 trucks and 3,400 anti-aircraft guns destroyed [H53].

The Trail grew regardless. After the PAVN's offensives in Laos in 1970 its corridor widened from about 30 to about 90 miles; by 1970 a petroleum pipeline from Vinh reached towards the A Shau; the PAVN built more than 3,000 km of roads and paths with bulldozers and graders, and floated fuel drums down the rivers [H53]. The phases' own estimates of net loss to the enemy's throughput fell from about 13.5 percent in Phase III to about 2 percent in Phase VI [H53]. It is the clearest case in the war of a metric improving without the war improving (A13): the trucks destroyed rose, and what arrived in the South rose with them. Over the war more than three million tons of ordnance fell on Laos [H53].

## ◆ EV000-69 · The Son Tay raid · 21 Nov 1970 · Son Tay prison camp, about 37 km west of Hanoi · HIST · 000
On the night of 20–21 November 1970 a joint task force under Brigadier General LeRoy J. Manor and Colonel Arthur D. Simons landed 56 Special Forces soldiers by HH-53 and HH-3E helicopters, guided by C-130 Combat Talons, at the prison camp at Son Tay to rescue about 61 American prisoners [H59]. Navy aircraft from USS *Oriskany* and USS *Ranger* flew a diversion over Haiphong, and F-105G Wild Weasels suppressed the SA-2 sites [H59]. The camp was empty: the prisoners had been moved in July, which intelligence learned only days before [H59]. The raiders lost two wounded, an HH-3E deliberately crash-landed inside the compound and an F-105G to a SAM; they reported 42 guards killed, a Vietnamese source six guards and seven civilians [H59]. The raid failed in its purpose but succeeded in another: Hanoi consolidated its prisoners in central prisons in Hanoi, and many returning prisoners said their treatment and morale improved [H59].

## ◆ EV000-70 · The Cooper–Church amendment · 29 Dec 1970 · Washington · HIST · 000
After the House had rejected the version passed by the Senate in June, the Cooper–Church amendment was enacted in December 1970 as part of the Supplementary Foreign Assistance Act and signed on 29 December [H55] [H56]. It barred US ground troops and advisers from operations in Laos and Cambodia [H55] [H56]. It wrote into law the sanctuary constraint that had been policy since 1965, at the moment the administration was planning to attack the Trail on the ground. Any operation into Laos would now be the ARVN's alone, without the American advisers who called in the air support and coordinated the helicopters on which ARVN operations depended.

## ◆ EV000-71 · Lam Son 719 · 8 Feb – 25 Mar 1971 · Route 9 from Khe Sanh to Tchepone, the Laotian panhandle (Base Areas 604 and 611) · HIST · 000
In Dewey Canyon II, beginning at the end of January, US forces reopened Route 9 to Khe Sanh inside South Vietnam [H56]. On 8 February ARVN I Corps under Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam attacked west along Route 9 into Laos towards Tchepone, with the 1st Infantry Division, the Airborne Division, the Marine Division, the 1st Armored Brigade and the 21st and 39th Ranger Battalions, to cut the Trail at Base Areas 604 and 611 in the dry season's peak [H56]. US Army helicopters flew more than 160,000 sorties in support and B-52s 1,358 sorties with 32,000 tons [H56]; no American advisers could go with the ARVN units [H56]. The PAVN, which had expected the attack, committed the B-70 Corps with the 304th, 308th and 320th Divisions, and the 2nd and 324B Divisions, with tanks and heavy anti-aircraft artillery [H56].

The advance stalled within days. Firebases north of Route 9 held by Rangers and Airborne were overrun or abandoned; on 6 March, in the largest helicopter assault of the war, the 2nd Regiment of the 1st Division was lifted towards Tchepone and entered the abandoned town on 7 March, and from 9 March the withdrawal began [H56]. It became a retreat under pressure, with the Marines' Fire Support Base Delta falling on 22 March and the images of ARVN soldiers clinging to helicopter skids reaching the world [H56] [H]. The last ARVN units were out by 25 March; Khe Sanh was abandoned again on 6 April [H56]. The Americans lost 215 killed, 1,149 wounded and 38 missing, and 108 helicopters destroyed and 618 damaged [H56]. South Vietnamese losses are given from 1,146 to 8,843 killed, a range that is itself a measure of the dispute; Saigon claimed 19,360 PAVN killed and Hanoi admits 2,163 killed and 6,176 wounded [H56]. Nixon said on 7 April that "Vietnamization has succeeded" [H56]. Hanoi read it otherwise, and the traffic on the Trail rose soon after [H56].

## ◆ EV000-72 · The war on trial at home · 29 Mar – 30 Jun 1971 · Fort Benning, Washington and New York · HIST · 000
On 29 March 1971 a court-martial at Fort Benning convicted Lieutenant Calley of the premeditated murder of at least 20 people at My Lai and sentenced him to life imprisonment; two days later Nixon ordered him moved to house arrest pending appeal [H47]. His sentence was later reduced, and he was paroled in 1974 [H47]. In April veterans opposed to the war demonstrated in Washington and threw their medals onto the Capitol steps [H]. On 13 June the *New York Times* began publishing the Pentagon Papers, the Defense Department's secret history of the war's decisions to 1968, leaked by Daniel Ellsberg; on 30 June the Supreme Court refused to stop publication [H]. The administration's response, the "plumbers" unit formed to stop leaks, led to Watergate [H]. By mid-1971 a majority of Americans told pollsters the war had been a mistake [H].

## ◆ EV000-73 · Thieu's unopposed re-election · Oct 1971 · Republic of Vietnam · HIST · 000
In the presidential election of October 1971 Thieu ran alone. Ky was at first disqualified under an election law requiring endorsements from deputies or provincial councillors, then reinstated by the Supreme Court, and withdrew; Duong Van Minh withdrew, charging that the election was rigged [H60] [H]. Thieu received all the valid votes, 5,971,114, and the reported turnout was 87.97 percent of 7,192,660 registered voters; valid ballots were 94.37 percent of those cast [H60]. A government that had won with a third of the vote in a contested election in 1967 was now returned in a referendum on itself. The army and administration remained Thieu's, and the regime was more stable than at any time since 1963; but its claim to stand for the whole non-communist South had narrowed, at the moment American forces were leaving it to stand alone.

## How the phase ends
At the end of 1971 the United States has about 158,000 military personnel in Vietnam, its ground combat role is nearly over, and the last US combat divisions are leaving [H40]. The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before [H62]. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960; and Land to the Tiller has begun to change the Delta [H63]. These gains are real, and they are measured mostly by indicators the government itself produces.

On the frontiers the balance is the reverse. The PAVN has rebuilt its main forces, extended the Trail in Laos and Cambodia, lost Sihanoukville and replaced it, and watched the ARVN's best divisions fail in Laos without American advisers. The secret channel in Paris is deadlocked on Thieu's removal and on the PAVN's presence in the South. In Hanoi, after Lam Son 719, the Politburo has decided to stake the next year on a conventional invasion across the DMZ, from Laos into the Central Highlands and from Cambodia towards Saigon, timed to an American election year and to the near completion of the American withdrawal [H56] [H]. The question of Phase V is the one Vietnamization was built to answer: whether the South can stop a PAVN conventional offensive with American air power but without American ground troops.

---

# Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

1972 is the test of Vietnamization, and the answer it gives is exact: the Republic of Vietnam can stop a full PAVN conventional offensive with American air power and American advisers, and cannot do it without them. On 30 March the PAVN opens the largest offensive of the war, called the Nguyen Hue Offensive in Hanoi and the Easter Offensive in the West, with about fourteen divisions and hundreds of tanks [H] on three main fronts: across the DMZ into Quang Tri, from Laos and Cambodia into the Central Highlands at Kontum, and from Cambodia down Route 13 at An Loc towards Saigon [H64]. US ground strength has fallen to about 69,000 men, few of them combat troops, and is on its way to 27,000 [H64]. US air power returns in strength: B-52s and tactical aircraft over the battlefields of the South, and, for the first time since 1968, a bombing campaign against the North without most of Rolling Thunder's restrictions, with the mining of Haiphong.

The shape of the phase is a near-collapse in the spring and a recovery in the summer. Quang Tri Province falls on 1–2 May; Kontum and An Loc are besieged and held by narrow margins and B-52s; and by the autumn the ARVN, under better commanders, has retaken Quang Tri City. The PAVN loses most of the armour it committed and, by most estimates, about 100,000 men, killed and wounded, while keeping about a tenth of the South's territory, mostly thinly populated border regions in the west [H64]. The offensive creates almost a million refugees and kills more than 25,000 civilians [H64]. Its political result is the one Hanoi needed: a settlement on terms that leave PAVN troops in the South. The year ends with the October draft agreement, Thieu's refusal of it, and the eleven days of Linebacker II.

## ◆ EV000-74 · The Easter Offensive opens: the DMZ front · 30 Mar – 2 Apr 1972 · Quang Tri Province, from the DMZ to the Cua Viet and Camp Carroll · HIST · 000
At midday on 30 March 1972 PAVN artillery, including 130mm guns that outranged anything the ARVN had, opened on the firebases strung along the DMZ, and the 304th and 308th Divisions with armoured regiments attacked across the demarcation line, while the 324B came in from the A Shau and the west [H64] [H67]. In all, PAVN forces on the northern front were supported by more than 100 tanks, T-54s, T-34s and PT-76s [H64]. The front was held by the ARVN 3rd Division under Brigadier General Vu Van Giai, a new division formed in late 1971 from mixed and unsteady units, with the 147th and 258th Vietnamese Marine Brigades under its control [H67] [H]. Low cloud kept most air support away for the first days [H64].

The firebases fell back or were overrun. On 2 April the 56th Regiment at Camp Carroll, under Lieutenant Colonel Pham Van Dinh, surrendered with about 1,500 men [H67]. That afternoon at Dong Ha, Captain John Ripley, US adviser to the 3rd Vietnamese Marine Battalion, spent about three hours under fire placing charges on the highway bridge over the Cua Viet, which was blown at 16:30 as PAVN tanks approached; the Marines held the river line [H67]. The PAVN halted to regroup and bring up supplies, and the 3rd Division, under fire from guns it could not reach, settled into a defence of Quang Tri City along the Thach Han and Cua Viet rivers.

## ◆ EV000-75 · Freedom Train, Pocket Money and Linebacker · 5 Apr – 23 Oct 1972 · North Vietnam, Haiphong harbour and the approaches to the DMZ · HIST · 000
On 5 April Nixon authorized strikes north of the 20th parallel, Operation Freedom Train, and on 10 April B-52s struck petroleum storage near Vinh [H68]. On 27 April and 13 May F-4s with laser-guided bombs dropped the span of the Thanh Hoa bridge that Rolling Thunder had failed to bring down, and on 10–11 May the Paul Doumer bridge at Hanoi was dropped the same way [H16] [H]. On 8 May (9 May in Vietnam) Nixon announced Operation Pocket Money, the mining of Haiphong and the other ports: Navy aircraft laid the mines, which were activated after five days, and about 11,000 more mines were sown in the secondary harbours and waterways over the following days [H68]. The mining of the northern ports, prohibited since 1965, closed the North's main entry point for Soviet supplies by sea.

Linebacker, from 10 May to 23 October, opened the North to bombing with targets chosen by the commanders rather than in Washington [H68]. On its first day, in 414 sorties, the heaviest air-to-air fighting of the war took place, and Lieutenant Randy Cunningham and Lieutenant (jg) William Driscoll became the first American aces of the war [H68]. Linebacker flew 41,653 missions and dropped 155,548 tons, and lost 134 aircraft, 104 in combat [H68]. Its effect was felt at the front: by a PAVN history only 30 percent of planned supplies reached its front-line units in May and June, the PAVN shelling of the South fell by half between 9 May and 1 June, and by September imports were 35–50 percent below the May level [H68]. The Soviet Union and China denounced the mining and did nothing; the Nixon–Brezhnev summit in Moscow went ahead from 22 May [H68] [H].

## ◆ EV000-76 · Loc Ninh and the siege of An Loc · 7 Apr – 18 Jun 1972 · Loc Ninh and An Loc, Binh Long Province, on Route 13 · HIST · 000
On 5 April the 5th Division of the PAVN B-2 Front attacked Loc Ninh, on Route 13 near the Cambodian border, and overran it on the afternoon of 7 April; the 9th Division took the Quan Loi base camp that evening, and the 7th Division cut Route 13 south of An Loc at the Tau O bridge with its 141st, 165th and 209th Regiments [H65]. An Loc, the provincial capital 100 km north of Saigon, was cut off by 8 April [H65]. It was held by the ARVN 5th Division under Brigadier General Le Van Hung, with the 3rd and 81st Ranger Groups, the 1st Airborne Brigade lifted in after failing to break through at Tau O, and the Regional Forces, Popular Forces and People's Self-Defence Force of Binh Long Province, all under III Corps (Lieutenant General Nguyen Van Minh) and advised by the American regional assistance command under Major General James Hollingsworth [H65].

The 9th Division assaulted on 13 April with tanks; in that first attack the defenders destroyed tanks with M72 LAWs at close range, and tank-killing teams were formed in every battalion [H65]. Further assaults followed in April and May. The town survived on airdrops, taken over by USAF C-130s on 19 April once anti-aircraft fire made helicopter landings impossible, and on air support, B-52s above all: on 11–12 May B-52s struck one mission every 55 minutes for 30 hours against the massed PAVN assault, with AC-119 and AC-130E gunships, A-37s and AH-1 Cobras [H65]. The 21st Division fought up Route 13 from Lai Khe [H65]. The PAVN was driven from the town by 12 June and III Corps declared the siege over on 18 June [H65] [H64]. US estimates of PAVN losses are 10,000 killed and 15,000 wounded and 36 tanks; Vietnamese figures are about 2,000 killed and 5,000 wounded [H65]. Brigadier General Richard Tallman, the deputy American commander, was mortally wounded by artillery on 9 July [H65]. An Loc lay in ruins. It became the symbol of an ARVN that could hold, if the B-52s came.

## ◆ EV000-77 · Tan Canh, Dak To and the battle of Kontum · 24 Apr – 9 Jun 1972 · Tan Canh, Dak To, Ben Het and Kontum city, Kontum Province · HIST · 000
In the Central Highlands the PAVN 320th Division began pressing the firebases on Rocket Ridge in early April, and on 24 April the 2nd Division's 1st and 66th Regiments, with the D10 Sapper Battalion and tanks, overran the ARVN bases at Tan Canh and Dak To II, held by the 42nd and 47th Regiments of the 22nd Division; the division "ceased to exist as a fighting unit", and its commander, Colonel Le Duc Dat, disappeared [H66]. The road to Kontum lay open. The PAVN paused for three weeks [H66]. John Paul Vann, the civilian director of the II Corps advisory effort, effectively directed the defence; he had Colonel Ly Tong Ba of the 23rd Division put in command of Kontum, and on 10 May Major General Nguyen Van Toan replaced Ngo Du at II Corps [H64] [H66]. On 9 May at Ben Het, ARVN Rangers destroyed three PT-76s with BGM-71 TOW missiles, among the first combat uses of the weapon, and TOW-armed helicopters followed [H66].

The main assault on Kontum came on 14 May, by the 320th Division's 48th, 52nd and 64th Regiments and the 2nd Division [H66] [H64]. B-52 strikes, on 14 May and decisively on the night of 16–17 May, fell close to the ARVN lines and broke the momentum of the attack [H66]. From 29 May to 8 June the ARVN cleared the city bunker by bunker, and on 9 June Ba, now a brigadier general, declared Kontum secure [H66]. That night Vann's helicopter flew into a hillside in low cloud and he was killed; a Vietnamese account says it was shot down [H66]. US estimates put PAVN casualties in the Kontum battle at about 4,000 and in the Highlands campaign at 20,000–40,000, figures with no better basis than the body counts of earlier years [H66].

## ◆ EV000-78 · The fall of Quang Tri · 27 Apr – 2 May 1972 · Quang Tri City and Highway 1 south to the My Chanh River · HIST · 000
On 27 April the PAVN renewed its attack on the 3rd Division's defence of Quang Tri City [H]. Contradictory orders from the I Corps commander, Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam, and from Giai left units moving in opposite directions, and on 1 May Giai ordered the city abandoned [H67] [H]. The division broke. Soldiers and refugees fled south on Highway 1, and PAVN artillery fired on the column, killing roughly 2,000 soldiers and civilians on the road [H67]. Quang Tri Province was lost by 2 May; the Marines who held at the My Chanh River were the one coherent force left north of Hue [H64] [H]. On 2 May Thieu relieved Lam and gave I Corps to Lieutenant General Ngo Quang Truong, who stopped the rout, restored order in Hue and held the My Chanh line with the Marine and Airborne Divisions and the 1st Division [H64]. Giai was later court-martialled and sentenced to five years' imprisonment [H64]. The fall of Quang Tri was the first loss of a province to a PAVN conventional offensive, and Truong's recovery the clearest demonstration of what leadership was worth in the ARVN.

## ◆ EV000-79 · The recapture of Quang Tri City · 28 Jun – 16 Sep 1972 · Quang Tri Province south of the Thach Han River and the Quang Tri Citadel · HIST · 000
On 28 June Truong opened the counter-offensive, Lam Son 72, with the Airborne Division and the Marine Division under Brigadier General Bui The Lan, whose 147th, 258th and 369th Marine Brigades did most of the fighting for the city [H70]. Against them were the 304th, 308th, 320B and 325th Divisions with the 312th identified [H70]. US forces provided fire and movement but no ground troops: in July alone, 5,461 tactical sorties and 2,054 B-52 strikes; US Marine helicopters of HMM-164 and HMM-165 lifted the Vietnamese Marines into landing zones, losing several to SA-7 missiles; and the 9th Marine Amphibious Brigade and the Seventh Fleet staged amphibious feints [H70]. The PAVN held the Quang Tri Citadel, its walls about 15 feet high, with interlocking tunnels and positions; the Marines breached the southeast wall on 10–11 September, held the Citadel by the late afternoon of 15 September, and raised the flag over the west gate on 16 September after 138 days of occupation [H70]. The city was rubble [H70].

The Marine Division lost 977 killed of 3,658 casualties, and the Airborne Division's 2nd Brigade was badly depleted [H70]. South Vietnamese claims are 8,135 PAVN killed; Hanoi's are 4,000–10,000 [H70]. About 20 Americans were killed [H70]. The province north of the Thach Han remained in PAVN hands, and both sides were too exhausted to move further [H70]. The battle proved that the ARVN's best divisions, under a good commander and with unlimited American fire support, could defeat the PAVN in a set-piece battle. Every one of those conditions was American or rare.

## ◆ EV000-80 · The last American ground combat units leave · Aug 1972 · South Vietnam · HIST · 000
In August 1972 the last US ground combat battalion in South Vietnam, the 3rd Battalion, 21st Infantry of the 196th Brigade, stood down at Da Nang and left the country [H]. American advisers, aviation units, the air and naval forces in and around Vietnam, and a shrinking logistics command remained, and US strength fell to about 24,000 by the end of the year [H40]. US deaths by hostile action fell to 300 in 1972 [H40]. The withdrawal begun at Midway in 1969 had been completed for the ground war during the largest PAVN offensive of the conflict, and the defence of the South on the ground had become entirely the RVNAF's. US air power, at its 1972 peak, was the part of the American commitment that remained.

## ◆ EV000-81 · The October agreement and Thieu's refusal · 8 Oct – 13 Dec 1972 · Paris, Saigon and Washington · HIST · 000
On 8 October Le Duc Tho presented Kissinger in Paris with a draft that dropped Hanoi's demand for Thieu's removal: a ceasefire in place, the withdrawal of all US forces within 60 days, the return of prisoners, the Thieu government to remain alongside the PRG pending a political settlement through a council of reconciliation, and no requirement for PAVN forces to leave the South [H51] [H]. Kissinger accepted it as the basis for an agreement. Thieu rejected it: it left the PAVN in his country and gave the PRG standing, and he had not been consulted in its drafting [H51] [H]. On 26 October Kissinger announced that "peace is at hand" [H]. On 7 November Nixon was re-elected, carrying 49 states [H]. Washington then sent Saigon a mass of equipment under Operation Enhance Plus, aircraft, armour and artillery, to be in the country before a ceasefire froze replacement at one-for-one, and Nixon gave Thieu private written assurances that the United States would respond with full force to a major violation [H] [H51].

In November and December Kissinger brought Saigon's amendments to Paris, Hanoi hardened its own terms in reply, and the main round of talks broke down on 13 December [H69]. Nixon, concerned that the new Congress in January would cut off the war's funding, gave Hanoi an ultimatum [H69].

## ◆ EV000-82 · Linebacker II · 18–29 Dec 1972 · Hanoi, Haiphong and their surroundings · HIST · 000
On 18 December B-52s attacked Hanoi and Haiphong for the first time in the war [H69]. In eleven days, with a 36-hour pause at Christmas, 741 B-52 sorties were dispatched and 729 completed against rail yards at Kinh No, Lang Dang and Yen Vien, power plants including Thai Nguyen, petroleum storage, airfields and SAM sites, dropping about 15,237 tons, and fighter-bombers added about 5,000 tons [H69]. The B-52s flew fixed routes and timings on the first nights and suffered for it [H]. North Vietnam fired 266 SA-2s over the eleven days [H69]. The United States acknowledged 15 B-52s shot down, and some authors argue for 22–27 counting damaged aircraft written off; 12 tactical aircraft were lost; 33 B-52 crewmen were killed or missing, 33 captured and 26 rescued [H69]. By the last nights US commanders judged the North's SA-2 stocks nearly exhausted and its air defences largely suppressed [H].

North Vietnam's official count of civilian dead is 1,624, 1,328 in Hanoi and 306 in Haiphong [H69]. The Bach Mai hospital was struck on 22 December, and on 26 December bombs on Kham Thien Street killed 278 by Hanoi's count [H69]. About 80 percent of the North's electrical generating capacity was put out of action [H69]. On 30 December Nixon halted the bombing north of the 20th parallel, and Hanoi agreed to resume talks, which reopened on 9 January 1973 [H69]. Whether the bombing forced Hanoi back to terms or merely covered the American acceptance of terms close to October's is disputed; Le Duan later said it had "completely obliterated our economic foundation" [H69].

## How the phase ends
At the end of 1972 the war is on the verge of a settlement that both governments in Vietnam regard as provisional. The Easter Offensive has failed to destroy the ARVN or the Thieu government, at a cost to the PAVN of most of the armour it committed (by one count 134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) and about 100,000 men [H64]. The ARVN has held at An Loc and Kontum and retaken Quang Tri City, but has lost Quang Tri north of the Thach Han, the western Highlands and the border areas of III Corps, and its losses are given variously from about 10,000 killed to about 39,000 dead in the period [H64]. Almost a million South Vietnamese have been made refugees, about 600,000 of them in government camps [H64].

The lesson both sides draw is the same. The ARVN held where American air power was decisive, at An Loc and Kontum, and where American advisers coordinated it; it broke where its leadership failed, at Quang Tri and Tan Canh. The settlement about to be signed removes the American advisers and the American air power and leaves the PAVN in the South, while the North's air defences and economy recover. Hanoi needs only to rebuild, wait for the Americans to be gone, and choose its time.

---

# Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

*End of phase against the historical state: as historical on every headline variable.*

Phase VI is the war without the Americans, and the end of the Republic of Vietnam. The Paris Agreement of January 1973 takes US forces out and returns the prisoners; it leaves the PAVN in the South, the Thieu government in Saigon, and the war to be decided between them. The ceasefire never holds. In 1973 Saigon is on the offensive, recovering hamlets and roads, while the North rebuilds; in 1974 the two are evenly matched, and the ARVN, short of ammunition, fuel and spare parts as American aid falls, bleeds in a war of attrition it cannot sustain; in January 1975 the North tests whether the United States will respond to the seizure of a province, and when it does not, it commits everything [H72].

The shape of the phase is three slow years and seven fast weeks. The constraints that bind the American role are now law, not policy: the Case–Church amendment ends all US combat activity in Indochina from 15 August 1973, the War Powers Resolution limits the President's power to send forces back, and Congress cuts military aid. Watergate removes the President who gave Thieu his assurances. In Hanoi, the 21st Plenum of October 1973 returns to revolutionary violence, and the PAVN builds a road network east of the mountains, a fuel pipeline into the South and an army of corps. In Saigon, the economy, hit by the oil shock and the departure of the Americans whose spending had sustained it, and a government that has narrowed its base, face the offensive of 1975 with an army spread thin across the whole country. When the blow falls at Ban Me Thuot in March, Thieu's decision to abandon the Highlands turns a defeat into a rout, and in eight weeks the Republic falls. The PAVN enters Saigon on 30 April 1975.

## ◆ EV000-83 · The Paris Agreement · 27 Jan 1973 · Paris · HIST · 000
On 27 January 1973 the Agreement on Ending the War and Restoring Peace in Vietnam was signed in Paris by the United States, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, the Republic of Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government [H51] [H]. A ceasefire in place took effect on 28 January Saigon time [H]. The United States and its allies would withdraw all forces within 60 days, and prisoners would be exchanged in the same period [H51]. Nothing required the PAVN to leave the South, where by US estimates about 150,000 of its troops remained [H51] [H]. The Thieu government remained, and a National Council of National Reconciliation and Concord was to arrange elections, which it never did [H]. An International Commission of Control and Supervision of Canadian, Hungarian, Indonesian and Polish personnel, and a Four-Party Joint Military Commission, were to supervise the ceasefire, and both sides could replace worn-out armaments one for one [H51] [H]. Thieu signed under American pressure, with Nixon's written promises of continued aid and of a forceful response to a major violation [H51]. The agreement was close to the terms of October 1972.

## ◆ EV000-84 · The ceasefire that never held · 28 Jan – Dec 1973 · The countryside of South Vietnam · HIST · 000
In the last days before the ceasefire both sides grabbed for hamlets and roads, raising flags to claim territory, the "war of the flags"; the ARVN recovered most of what the PAVN and VC had seized [H]. Fighting resumed in earnest by March [H51]. Through most of 1973 the Saigon government was on the offensive: the Communists, rebuilding supply lines and wary of provoking the return of American air power, largely stayed on the defensive, while the ARVN and territorial forces pushed into PRG-held areas [H72]. Both sides violated the agreement from the start; the ICCS could not stop it, and Canada left the commission in July 1973 [H]. From late 1973 the PAVN grew bolder as the American political system turned on itself, and by early 1974 the two sides fought roughly on equal terms [H72].

## ◆ EV000-85 · Operation Homecoming and the last American troops · 12 Feb – 29 Mar 1973 · Hanoi, Clark Air Base and Saigon · HIST · 000
On 12 February 1973 the first American prisoners were flown out of Hanoi to Clark Air Base in the Philippines [H78]. By 29 March, 566 US servicemen, 23 American civilians and 5 foreign nationals had come home through Clark [H78]. On 29 March 1973 the last US combat and support troops left South Vietnam, and MACV was disestablished [H]. A Defense Attaché Office under Major General John E. Murray, with a few dozen military personnel and civilian contractors, took over the management of American military aid [H]. The United States still maintained air power in Thailand and the Seventh Fleet offshore, and continued to bomb in Cambodia [H]. The question of Americans missing in action, about whom Hanoi gave little information, would keep the war alive in American politics for two decades [H].

## ◆ EV000-86 · Case–Church and the end of American combat in Indochina · Jun – 7 Nov 1973 · Washington; Cambodia · HIST · 000
In June 1973 Congress passed the Case–Church amendment, which barred any US military activity in or over Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia without congressional approval from 15 August 1973 [H51] [H]. On 15 August the bombing of Cambodia, which had continued since the Paris Agreement, ended [H]. On 7 November Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto, limiting the President's power to commit forces to hostilities without Congress [H]. Nixon's promise to Thieu of a forceful response to a major violation was now beyond the President's power to keep without Congress, and Congress would not give it [H]. The sanctuary constraint, which had shaped the war since 1964, now covered the whole of Indochina and was written into law.

## ◆ EV000-87 · Resolution 21 and the North's rebuilding · Oct 1973 – 1974 · Hanoi; the Laotian panhandle and the western Highlands · HIST · 000
In October 1973 the 21st Plenum of the Party Central Committee in Hanoi resolved that the revolution in the South must continue by the path of revolutionary violence, and that the PAVN should respond to Saigon's operations and prepare for a decisive offensive [H]. The PAVN rebuilt through 1973 and 1974: it improved the strategic road along the western side of South Vietnam east of the Truong Son, extended the fuel pipeline into the South, built up stocks of ammunition and armour in the base areas and grouped its divisions into army corps, the 1st Corps in October 1973 and the 4th Corps on 20 July 1974 among them [H] [H73]. It was the North's own decision, on its own reading of the American political collapse and Saigon's weakness, and it was taken while Saigon still held the initiative in the countryside.

## ◆ EV000-88 · Saigon declares the war resumed; the Paracels · Jan 1974 · Saigon; the Paracel Islands · HIST · 000
In January 1974 Thieu announced that the war had resumed and that the Paris Agreement no longer bound his forces [H51] [H]. On 19 January a Chinese naval force defeated South Vietnamese ships in the Paracel Islands, and China took control of the islands [H71]. The United States did not intervene [H]. The clash showed how isolated Saigon had become: its ally would not act, and a great power on its northern horizon was willing to take territory from it.

## ◆ EV000-89 · The aid cuts and the shortages · 25 Jan – 9 Aug 1974 · South Vietnam and Washington · HIST · 000
On 25 January 1974 supplies of ammunition and fuel to all ARVN units were cut because of budget limits [H71]. US military aid fell from about $1.1 billion in fiscal year 1974 to an appropriation of about $700 million for fiscal year 1975, the July 1974–June 1975 year, the figure given by source as $700–750 million [H72] [H71]. Major General Murray of the Defense Attaché Office warned that cuts in support could roughly be equated with loss of territory, and that aid of $600 million would mean writing the South off [H71]. The ARVN rationed artillery rounds, grounded aircraft and helicopters for lack of fuel and parts, and cut patrols; the soldiers' pay lost most of its value to inflation, and desertion rose [H]. The economy suffered from the world oil shock of late 1973 and the loss of American spending [H]. On 9 August 1974 Nixon resigned over Watergate, and Gerald Ford succeeded him [H71]. The President who had given Thieu written promises was gone.

## ◆ EV000-90 · The ARVN's last offensives · 12 Feb – 2 May 1974 · Tri Phap, Dinh Tuong Province; Svay Rieng, Cambodia · HIST · 000
In the spring of 1974 the ARVN still had the strength to attack. From 12 February to 4 May it struck the PAVN base at Tri Phap in Dinh Tuong Province in the Delta [H71]. From 27 March to 2 May, in the last major ARVN offensive of the war, III Corps attacked the PAVN base areas around Svay Rieng in Cambodia, claiming more than 1,200 PAVN killed against fewer than 100 ARVN [H71]. They were the work of an army still able to win local battles when it had the ammunition and air support to do so. They did not change the balance, and after the spring the ARVN was on the defensive everywhere.

## ◆ EV000-91 · The war of attrition of 1974 · 16 May – 10 Dec 1974 · The Iron Triangle; Thuong Duc, Duc Duc and Phu Loc in I Corps · HIST · 000
From May 1974 the PAVN took the initiative with a series of "strategic raids" designed to grind down the ARVN and test its reserves [H] [H71]. In III Corps the PAVN 9th Division attacked Rach Bap in the Iron Triangle from 16 May; the ARVN retook it only in November [H71]. In I Corps a PAVN regiment overran An Hoa and attacked the district town of Thuong Duc from 18 July; the Airborne Division held the heights around it in a costly victory that lasted until November [H71]. At Duc Duc, from 18 July to 4 October, the ARVN 3rd Division suffered 4,700 casualties [H71]. From 28 August to 10 December the PAVN seized hills near Phu Loc that closed Phu Bai airfield to traffic and cut Highway 1, and the ARVN recovered them at heavy cost [H71]. In 1974 South Vietnam lost about 30,000 killed; the US estimated about 61,000 PAVN and VC killed [H71]. The ARVN, unable to replace its losses or its expended ammunition, had committed its strategic reserve, the Airborne and Marine Divisions, to static defence in I Corps, and had nothing left to move.

## ◆ EV000-92 · The fall of Phuoc Long · 12 Dec 1974 – 6 Jan 1975 · Phuoc Long Province (Phuoc Binh and Song Be), III Corps · HIST · 000
On 12 December 1974 the PAVN 4th Corps under Hoang Cam, with the 7th Division, the new 3rd Division and independent regiments including the 141st, 165th, 201st and 271st, and two armoured companies with 14 T-54s, attacked Phuoc Long Province on the Cambodian border [H73]. It was defended mainly by Regional Force battalions, reinforced by the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 7th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 9th Regiment of the 5th Division and the 81st Airborne Ranger Battalion [H73]. The last ARVN post fell on 6 January 1975, the first provincial capital lost permanently since the Paris Agreement [H73] [H]. The ARVN lost more than 1,000 killed and 2,444 captured; the PAVN about 1,300 killed and wounded [H73]. Saigon did not try to retake it. Washington made no military response [H73]. In Hanoi, where a strategy conference sat from 18 December to 8 January, Phuoc Long answered the question the leadership had set itself: the United States would not return [H71] [H]. The plan for a two-year campaign to end the war in 1976 was adapted to strike in the Central Highlands in 1975 [H].

## ◆ EV000-93 · The fall of Ban Me Thuot · 10–12 Mar 1975 · Ban Me Thuot, Darlac Province · HIST · 000
For Campaign 275 the PAVN Central Highlands Front under Lieutenant General Hoang Minh Thao, directed by the chief of the general staff, General Van Tien Dung, massed the 10th, 316th and 320A Divisions with the 3rd and 968th Divisions, tanks, artillery and anti-aircraft units [H74]. Diversionary attacks on Pleiku and Kontum, false radio traffic and local rumours drew the attention of the II Corps commander, Major General Pham Van Phu, who discounted repeated warnings and kept his forces in the north [H74]. At 02:00 on 10 March the PAVN attacked Ban Me Thuot, defended mainly by the 53rd Regiment of the 23rd Division with Rangers and Regional Forces; the town was in PAVN hands by 11–12 March [H74]. The counter-attack by the rest of the 23rd Division, lifted in by helicopter, was broken [H]. The PAVN admitted 600–800 killed and 2,416 wounded; the Vietnamese official history counts 28,514 ARVN put out of action, 4,502 killed and 16,822 captured [H74]. II Corps lost more than three-quarters of its combat units [H74]. Ban Me Thuot was the strategic surprise of the war's last campaign.

## ◆ EV000-94 · The collapse of I Corps · 13–30 Mar 1975 · Quang Tri, Hue and Da Nang · HIST · 000
On 13 March Thieu ordered Truong to give up most of I Corps and withdrew the Airborne Division towards Saigon as a reserve [H75]. On 20 March he ordered Truong to hold only Da Nang; on 29 March he ordered him to turn back and retake it, which Truong refused [H75]. The contradictory orders, given as the PAVN 2nd Corps with the 304th, 324th and 325th Divisions attacked from the north and west and the 2nd Division and 52nd Brigade struck in Quang Ngai and Quang Tin, broke I Corps [H75]. Northern Quang Tri was lost by 18 March; Hue was surrounded by the evening of 25 March and abandoned; about 6,000 soldiers of the 2nd Division deserted on 28 March; and the PAVN entered Da Nang on the afternoon of 29 March [H75]. Soldiers abandoned their units to find their families, and the sea evacuation from Da Nang became chaos, with people fighting to board the ships [H75]. I Corps had about 134,000 men against more than 75,000 PAVN and VC; three ARVN infantry divisions and the 147th Marine Brigade ceased to exist, and about 58,722 soldiers were captured at Hue [H75]. The PAVN took 129 aircraft, 179 armoured vehicles and 327 artillery pieces [H75]. The best corps in the ARVN, under its best commander, had been destroyed without a decisive battle.

## ◆ EV000-95 · The retreat from the Highlands · 14–25 Mar 1975 · Pleiku and Kontum to the coast along Route 7, through Cheo Reo · HIST · 000
On 14 March at Cam Ranh, Thieu ordered Phu to abandon Pleiku and Kontum and pull II Corps back to the coast to defend the populated regions [H74]. The chief of the Joint General Staff, General Cao Van Vien, warned against Route 19 because of the French disaster at the Mang Yang Pass in 1954; Thieu chose Route 7, a disused road in poor condition [H74]. The retreat was ordered verbally and kept secret, even from many of the units and the province chiefs; within days some 400,000 civilians had joined the columns [H74]. The PAVN ambushed the column near Cheo Reo, where fighting ended on 19 March, and shelled it along the road [H74]. Only the 6th Ranger Battalion and the 19th Armoured Cavalry Squadron arrived in good order; an estimated 155,000 civilians were killed or abducted on the "convoy of tears", and RVNAF air strikes hit civilians too [H74]. It was the decision that lost the war in the shortest time: II Corps, which had held the Highlands through every offensive since 1965, was destroyed on the road in ten days.

## ◆ EV000-96 · Xuan Loc · 9–21 Apr 1975 · Xuan Loc, Long Khanh Province, northeast of Saigon · HIST · 000
On 9 April the PAVN 4th Corps under Major General Hoang Cam, with the 6th, 7th and 341st Divisions and tanks and artillery, attacked Xuan Loc, the road junction northeast of Saigon on Route 1 [H76]. The town was held by the ARVN 18th Division under Brigadier General Le Minh Dao, with the 1st Airborne Brigade, armoured units, Rangers and Regional Forces, and air support from Bien Hoa and Tan Son Nhut [H76]. The 18th Division held for twelve days against repeated assaults; on 12 April two BLU-82 bombs were dropped on PAVN troops, reportedly killing about 200 [H76]. The PAVN changed its approach, bypassed and isolated the town, and on 19 April the Joint General Staff ordered the withdrawal; Xuan Loc was abandoned on 21 April, and the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Airborne Brigade was destroyed in the withdrawal at Suoi Ca [H76]. The PAVN claimed 2,036 ARVN killed or wounded and 2,731 captured and admitted 460 killed and 1,428 wounded; Americans estimated about 5,000 PAVN casualties and 37 tanks destroyed [H76]. On 17 April Phnom Penh fell to the Khmer Rouge [H]. Xuan Loc was the ARVN's last stand, and showed what a well-led division could still do; it bought twelve days.

## ◆ EV000-97 · Thieu resigns; the last governments of the Republic · 10–28 Apr 1975 · Saigon and Washington · HIST · 000
On 10 April President Ford asked Congress for $722 million in emergency military aid to rebuild some of the destroyed South Vietnamese forces; Congress would not vote it [H77] [H]. On 23 April Ford told an audience at Tulane University that the war was "finished as far as America is concerned" [H]. On 21 April Thieu resigned in a televised address denouncing the United States for abandoning his country, and handed power to Vice President Tran Van Huong [H77]. Thieu left the country a few days later [H]. On 28 April Huong handed the presidency to General Duong Van Minh, in the hope that Hanoi would negotiate with him; it would not [H77]. On 28 April captured A-37s flown by defecting pilots bombed Tan Son Nhut [H77].

## ◆ EV000-98 · The fall of Saigon · 29–30 Apr 1975 · Saigon · HIST · 000
By late April five PAVN corps, Group 232 and the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Corps, with 15 infantry divisions and three tank regiments, encircled Saigon in the Ho Chi Minh Campaign [H77]. Rockets and artillery hit Tan Son Nhut on the morning of 29 April; two US Marine guards, Corporal Charles McMahon and Lance Corporal Darwin Judge, were killed, the last American servicemen killed in action in Vietnam [H]. At 10:51 Operation Frequent Wind began: Marine and Air Force helicopters lifted 395 Americans and more than 4,000 Vietnamese from the Defense Attaché Office compound, and 978 Americans and about 1,100 Vietnamese from the embassy roof and grounds, to the ships of the Seventh Fleet [H77]. Ambassador Graham Martin left on a helicopter at 04:58 on 30 April [H77]. Thousands of Vietnamese who had worked with the Americans were left behind [H].

At 10:24 on 30 April Minh announced an unconditional surrender [H77]. PAVN tanks crashed through the gates of the Presidential Palace, Tank 390 through the main gate, and at 11:30 a soldier raised the flag of the Front over the palace [H77]. The Republic of Vietnam had ceased to exist. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City; Vietnam was formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976 [H].

## How the phase ends
The war ends on 30 April 1975 with the fall of Saigon and the unconditional surrender of the Republic of Vietnam, on the historical timeline: rung (a), collapse. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat and the limits on the President into law; American military aid had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963 but narrowly based, economically weakened and dependent on American supply, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment. The decisive blows were Hanoi's, at Phuoc Long and Ban Me Thuot; the decisive errors were Saigon's, in the order to abandon the Highlands and the contradictory orders to I Corps.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the Ho Chi Minh Campaign, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead [H]. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans [H]. That is the war as it happened, and the war the exercise begins from.
